items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend messages on Thursday afternoon: lunch on Saturday? You want to go. You also have work that day. In English you would say "I can't, I've got work on Saturday" — and notice that the *because* buried in there is doing quiet, factual work. You are not arguing your case or pushing back on the invitation. You are putting a fact on the table and letting it explain itself. Japanese has a joint built for exactly that move, and it is ので.

```jp
土[ど]曜[よう]日[ひ]は仕[し]事[ごと]があるので、日[にち]曜[よう]日[ひ]に会[あ]います。
```

*I have work on Saturday, so we'll meet on Sunday.*

Look at the shape for a second rather than the words. The reason comes first. ので sits at the seam. The result follows. One sentence, two halves, nobody raising their voice. That order is not a stylistic preference you get to play with — it is the pattern itself, and putting the halves the wrong way round is the single most common way this goes wrong in the first week.

## How it works

ので is two small pieces stuck together, and once you see which two, almost everything about its behaviour becomes predictable instead of memorised.

The の is a **nominalizer** — a little word that takes a whole clause and turns it into a thing you can point at. The で is the same で you already use for *by means of*: タクシーで is "by taxi". So 仕[し]事[ごと]があるので packages up "there is work" into a single thing, and then says "by that thing". You are not pleading a case. You are naming a fact and letting it sit there.

That is also the intuition for the register. Because the reason arrives pre-packaged as a thing rather than asserted as a claim, ので comes out neutral and slightly soft. It is the connector of timetables, of doctor's notes, and of politely getting out of Saturday lunch.

### Verbs and い-adjectives attach directly

Put the first clause in plain form — dictionary form, plain past, plain negative — and stick ので on the end. Nothing changes shape.

```jp
雨[あめ]が降[ふ]るので、傘[かさ]を持[も]ちます。
今日[きょう]はとても寒[さむ]いので、コートを着[き]ます。
```

*It's going to rain, so I'll take an umbrella.*
*It's very cold today, so I'll wear a coat.*

降[ふ]る is a bare dictionary form. 寒[さむ]い is a bare い-adjective. Neither one needs any help. A good working test: if the first half could stand on its own as a short, plain sentence, you can bolt ので onto it and keep going.

### Nouns and な-adjectives need な first

This is the one place where everybody slips, usually for about a week, so it is worth understanding rather than drilling. A noun or a な-adjective cannot touch ので directly. Remember that the の in there is a real の — the same one in 私[わたし]の本[ほん] — and it wants something in front of it that is already shaped to modify. Nouns and な-adjectives take that shape with な.

So 静[しず]か becomes 静[しず]かなので, and 子[こ]供[ども] becomes 子[こ]供[ども]なので.

```jp
この部屋[へや]は静[しず]かなので、よく勉[べん]強[きょう]します。
妹[いもうと]はまだ子[こ]供[ども]なので、お酒[さけ]を飲[の]みません。
```

*This room is quiet, so I study a lot.*
*My little sister is still a child, so she doesn't drink alcohol.*

That is where the form なので comes from, and it is why you will see なので written up as though it were a second, separate pattern. It is not. It is ので with the connector its own grammar demands, and nothing more.

### ので itself never conjugates

Tense, negation and politeness all live in the clause in front of ので. ので has no past form, no negative form, and no polite form of its own. That is genuinely good news: there is nothing extra to learn here, only something to leave alone.

```jp
昨日[きのう]は頭[あたま]が痛[いた]かったので、早[はや]く寝[ね]ました。
意[い]味[み]が分[わ]からないので、先[せん]生[せい]に質[しつ]問[もん]します。
```

*My head hurt yesterday, so I went to bed early.*
*I don't understand the meaning, so I'm going to ask the teacher.*

痛[いた]かった is past. 分[わ]からない is negative. ので does not react to either of them. The same holds for nouns and な-adjectives in the past: 学[がく]生[せい]だったので and 元[げん]気[き]だったので are both correct, and notice that the な has quietly disappeared in those — だった has already done the connecting work, so nothing else is needed.

What is never correct is `学生だので`. Plain だ cannot sit in front of ので at all, and な exists precisely to fill that gap.

### The polite exception: ますので and ですので

Here is a rule that ので politely breaks. Normally the polite endings ます and です live only at the very end of a sentence, and any clause sitting before a connector drops down to plain form. ので is one of the very few connectors that lets you keep the polite ending in the first half.

```jp
電[でん]車[しゃ]が遅[おく]れますので、タクシーで行[い]きます。
```

*The train is going to be late, so I'll go by taxi.*

遅[おく]れるので is completely correct, and it is what you will say most of the time. 遅[おく]れますので is a register dial, not a correction: it lifts the whole sentence into announcement territory — station platforms, shop staff, an email to somebody well above you. After a noun the same move gives you ですので, as in 今日[きょう]は雨[あめ]ですので.

Reach for the polite version when you are addressing a customer, a stranger you want to be careful with, or a whole room. Use the plain version with everybody else, or you will sound like you are reading off a laminated card.

## Rules and exceptions

> The reason always comes first. ので is a seam in the middle of one sentence, not a word you can slide to the end and hope for the best.

The sharp edges, roughly in the order you will hit them:

- `寒いなので` is wrong. An い-adjective already ends in something the の can grab, and adding な is like fitting a second hinge to a door that swings fine.
- `静かので` and `学生ので` are wrong for the mirror reason — those two are exactly the cases that do need な.
- `学生だので` is wrong. だ never appears in front of ので. If you catch yourself writing だ there, swap it for な and move on.
- In writing, ので does not begin a sentence. It joins two halves, so if there is no first half, there is nothing for it to join.

There is a softer rule about the second half too. Because ので presents its reason as a plain fact rather than as an argument, it sits comfortably in front of requests, apologies and quiet announcements, and it is the safe default whenever you are explaining yourself to somebody you do not know well. That softness is the entire reason the pattern earns its keep.

> That last written rule leaks badly in real life. Plenty of people start a fresh sentence with なので, using it much the way an English speaker opens with "So…". A teacher will mark it. Everybody says it anyway. Hold both facts at once.

One more piece of honest mess, and it will do more for you than any drill: a ので clause can be left hanging with nothing after it at all. That is not an unfinished sentence — it is a politeness move. You state the fact, you trail off, and you let the other person finish the thought in their own head. A large share of how adults decline invitations in Japanese is exactly this shape.

## Casual speech

In relaxed, fast speech ので contracts to んで. Same attachment rules, same meaning, much lower register.

```jp
ちょっと用[よう]事[じ]があるので、失[しつ]礼[れい]します。
ちょっと用[よう]事[じ]があるんで、また明日[あした]。
```

*I've got something to take care of, so I'll be off.*
*I've got a thing on, so — see you tomorrow.*

The first line is what you say standing up from a meeting: still polite, still a complete sentence. The second is what you say to a friend on the way out the door, and it is doing that trailing-off thing on purpose — the fact is stated, the apology is implied, and nobody has to say anything awkward out loud.

One warning about the contraction. なので shrinks to なんで, which is also how people say 何[なに]で, "why". Context sorts it out almost every time, and *almost* is the honest word. If a sentence with なんで in the middle suddenly refuses to make sense as a question, try reading it as a squashed なので instead.

## One sentence, or two

ので is the first connector of this kind you are meeting, so the useful contrast is not against another connector — it is against not using one at all. You already have だから and それで, and they do a related job from outside the sentence. Compare 今日[きょう]は忙[いそが]しいです。だから、行[い]きません。 with 今日[きょう]は忙[いそが]しいので、行[い]きません。

The first version is two separate sentences. You assert that you are busy, full stop, and then you announce a consequence of it. It is punchier and faintly more combative, because the reason got its own moment standing there as a claim that somebody could disagree with.

The second version is one sentence. Your being busy never gets asserted on its own — it arrives already folded into the background, and the actual point of the sentence is that you are not going. That is why ので feels smoother inside an apology, and why だから can read like the opening move of an argument. Neither one is more correct than the other. They simply put the weight in different places, and you now have both.

## The short version

Plain form plus ので. な after nouns and な-adjectives. Reason first, result second. ので itself never changes, and in polite settings the first half is allowed to stay in ます or です form.

Hold onto the shape of that の, because it comes back very soon. Swap the で for に and you get のに — the same clause turned into a thing, but the sentence flips from "this followed from that" to "this happened in spite of that", and the whole tone turns over with it.
caution_notes: Nouns and な-adjectives need な before ので (学生なので, 静かなので) — 学生ので and 学生だので are both wrong.
い-adjectives and plain verbs attach straight to ので, so 寒いなので is an over-correction.
The reason clause always comes first; ので is a seam inside one sentence, not a sentence opener in writing.
ので never conjugates — tense, negation and politeness all belong to the clause in front of it.

items.explanation_markdown:
You spend the whole morning making lunch for a friend who is coming over, and when they finally walk in they tell you they ate something on the way. English hands you "but". Japanese hands you something with more feeling packed into it.

```jp
昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]を作[つく]ったのに、友[とも]達[だち]はもう食[た]べました。
```

*Even though I made lunch, my friend had already eaten.*

のに joins two halves that refuse to fit together. The first half sets up what should logically have followed; the second half walks straight over it. And it never does that neutrally — のに always carries your reaction to the mismatch: disappointment, irritation, or plain surprise. That feeling is not decoration you can strip off. It is half of what the word means.

## How it works

のに attaches to the **plain form** — the plain form is the shape a word has before you add です or ます, the shape you would find in a dictionary. Dictionary form, past, negative: all of those are plain forms, and のに clips onto the end of any of them without changing them.

Verbs are the easy case. Nothing is removed, nothing shifts.

- 行[い]く → 行[い]くのに
- 行[い]った → 行[い]ったのに
- 行[い]かない → 行[い]かないのに

So a month of evenings can be undone in one short sentence:

```jp
毎[まい]日[にち]勉[べん]強[きょう]したのに、全[ぜん]然[ぜん]分[わ]かりません。
```

*Even though I studied every day, I don't understand at all.*

It is worth knowing why the word is built from の and に, because the shape explains the feeling. The の packages the entire first clause into a single thing — *the fact that I studied every day* — and the に plants that thing down as the background the rest of the sentence has to live with. You make the first half solid, then you show reality ignoring it. Frustration is the natural result of doing that.

い-adjectives behave exactly like verbs: 安[やす]い → 安[やす]いのに, 安[やす]かった → 安[やす]かったのに.

```jp
この店[みせ]は安[やす]いのに、料[りょう]理[り]がおいしいです。
```

*Even though this shop is cheap, the food is delicious.*

Notice that the surprise here is a happy one. のに is not only for complaints. It covers anything that lands somewhere you did not expect it to land, including good news.

Now the part that costs people points on tests. **な-adjectives and nouns need な in front of のに.** Both of them end in だ in their plain form (上手[じょうず]だ, 学[がく]生[せい]だ), and that だ cannot survive next to のに. It becomes な.

- 上手[じょうず]だ → 上手[じょうず]なのに
- 学[がく]生[せい]だ → 学[がく]生[せい]なのに

```jp
兄[あに]は英[えい]語[ご]が上手[じょうず]なのに、あまり話[はな]しません。
```

*Even though my older brother is good at English, he hardly speaks it.*

```jp
今日[きょう]は日[にち]曜[よう]日[ひ]なのに、父[ちち]は会[かい]社[しゃ]へ行[い]きました。
```

*Even though it's Sunday today, my father went to the office.*

That な is strictly a non-past thing. In the past, these same words end in だった, and だった is an ordinary plain form, so のに hooks straight onto it: 学[がく]生[せい]だったのに, 静[しず]かだったのに. There is no な in sight. People who over-apply the rule end up writing `学生だったなのに`, which nobody says out loud. The short version worth memorising: な shows up only where a bare だ would otherwise have been standing.

Writing `上手だのに` or `学生だのに` is the most common mistake with this pattern, and dropping the な altogether — `静かのに` — is the second. If ので is already comfortable for you, you get this for free: ので takes な in exactly the same two places (静[しず]かなので, 学[がく]生[せい]なので). Same joint, opposite message.

One more mechanical point. **Politeness lives at the end of the sentence, not at のに.** The first half stays plain even when the ending is polite: 勉[べん]強[きょう]したのに、分[わ]かりません is right, and `勉強しましたのに` is not something you want to write. This is normal across Japanese — the polite marker sits once, at the very end, and covers the whole sentence.

Order matters too, and it is fixed: the clause carrying のに is the setup, and the thing that defies it always comes afterwards. 兄[あに]は英[えい]語[ご]が上手[じょうず]なのに、あまり話[はな]しません puts the expectation first and the letdown second. Swap the halves and you have written a genuinely different sentence — あまり話[はな]さないのに、英[えい]語[ご]が上手[じょうず]です makes his silence the setup and his skill the surprise. Both are good Japanese. They simply aim the astonishment at different targets, so decide which half is the surprise before you start writing.

## The sharp edges

Here is the rule that catches everybody: **you cannot put a request, a command, or an invitation after のに.** のに reports a mismatch that already exists in the world; it has no power to lean on somebody. So `寒いのに窓を閉めてください` is broken Japanese, even though the English "it's cold, so please close the window" feels like it should map straight across. What that sentence needs is a reason, not a contrast:

```jp
寒[さむ]いので、窓[まど]を閉[し]めてください。
```

*It's cold, so please close the window.*

> Anything you ask, suggest, or order goes after ので, never after のに. If the back half of your sentence tells somebody to do something, のに is the wrong tool.

The second sharp edge is social rather than grammatical. Because のに always carries feeling, that feeling points at whoever caused the mismatch. Saying 医[い]者[しゃ]なのに to somebody's face is not a neutral observation — it is a complaint that they are a doctor and are not behaving like one. Between friends that is completely normal. Aimed upward at your boss, it is a small landmine.

> A のに sentence aimed at the person you are talking to reads as criticism, however soft your tone. Use it about situations and about yourself freely; use it about your listener carefully.

And one honest piece of mess, because Japanese does not keep its words in tidy boxes. The same string のに shows up doing a completely different job, where の is only a nominalizer — a small word that turns a verb phrase into a thing — and に marks purpose. You meet it after a dictionary-form verb when the back half of the sentence talks about how much time, money, or effort something took: 漢[かん]字[じ]を覚[おぼ]えるのに時[じ]間[かん]を使[つか]いました. There is no contrast anywhere in that sentence and no feeling attached. The giveaway is what the second half is about, not the shape of the words, so read to the end of the sentence before you decide which のに you are looking at. This one confuses everybody once and then never again.

## In casual speech

のに does not contract. What it does in real conversation is stop early. People say the first half, arrive at のに, and simply quit — the second half is obvious to everyone in the room, and leaving it unsaid hits harder than finishing it.

```jp
約[やく]束[そく]したのに。
```

*And you promised...*

There is no main clause in that sentence at all, and it does not need one. Everybody present knows exactly what did not happen. In relaxed speech you will also hear のにな and のになあ tacked on the end — 約[やく]束[そく]したのになあ — which turns the complaint into something closer to a sigh, more disappointed than angry.

## のに against ので

You learned ので as a plain, neutral "because". のに is built on the same joint and points the opposite way. Watch what a single syllable does to the same scene:

```jp
今日[きょう]は寒[さむ]いので、彼[かれ]はコートを着[き]ました。
今日[きょう]は寒[さむ]いのに、彼[かれ]はコートを着[き]ませんでした。
```

*It's cold today, so he put on a coat.*
*Even though it's cold today, he didn't put on a coat.*

The first sentence describes a world that behaves. Cold weather, coat, no comment from you — ので simply says the second half follows from the first. The second sentence describes a world that misbehaves, and you clearly have an opinion about it. のに says the second half defies the first, and adds *and I noticed*.

A useful test while this is still new: after you write のに, try adding "and I am not happy about it" to the English of your sentence. If that fits the mood you wanted, you picked correctly. If the contrast is flat and factual and you honestly do not care, のに will land heavier than you meant it to.

The machinery, happily, is identical between the two. Both attach to the plain form, both turn a bare だ into な after a noun or a な-adjective, and both leave the politeness sitting at the far end of the sentence. So the only real decision in front of you is direction: does the second half follow from the first, or does it defy it? Answer that honestly and the shape looks after itself.

Plain form plus のに, な after nouns and な-adjectives, nothing you can ask for on the other side, and always a feeling attached. Hold onto that unfinished 約[やく]束[そく]したのに — when you meet たら for "if" a little later, it slots into exactly that hanging position to build the Japanese equivalent of "I wish...".
caution_notes: After a noun or a な-adjective, change だ to な before のに (学生なのに).
Never follow a のに clause with a request, a command, or an invitation — use ので for those.
のに always carries disappointment, irritation, or surprise, so aiming one at your listener sounds like criticism.
Keep the clause in front of のに plain; the polite ending belongs only at the end of the sentence.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend texts you from the other side of town: the new shop by the station is cheap, the food is good, go. You have never set foot in it. The next day someone asks you where to eat, and here is the problem. If you say あの新[あたら]しい店[みせ]は安[やす]いです, you are speaking as though you walked in and checked the prices yourself. You did not. You are relaying somebody else's report, and Japanese would like you to say so out loud.

That is the whole job of そうだ. You build the sentence exactly the way you would say it plainly, and then you park そうだ on the end.

```jp
あの新[あたら]しい店[みせ]は安[やす]いそうです。
```

*I hear that new shop is cheap.*

One small ending, and the sentence changes owner. The content is unchanged — cheap shop, still cheap — but you have stepped back from it and handed the responsibility to whoever told you. Adults spend a startling amount of conversation on things they did not personally witness, so this ending earns its keep fast.

## How it works

The rule fits on one line: **plain form + そうだ**. The plain form is the dictionary-style form, the one with no です or ます hanging off it. It carries all the tense and all the negation. そうだ sits behind it and never moves.

Verbs are the easy case. Take the plain form, whatever it is, and clip そうだ onto the back.

```jp
兄[あに]は来[らい]年[ねん]日本[にほん]に行[い]くそうです。
```

*I hear my older brother is going to Japan next year.*

Notice that nothing about 行[い]く changed. There is no special "hearsay form" to learn — you already know how to make the plain forms, so you already know how to do this. Past and negative go on the verb, never on そうだ. If the report is about something that did not happen, the verb goes negative and そうだ carries on exactly as before.

```jp
彼[かれ]は昨日[きのう]の会[かい]議[ぎ]に来[こ]なかったそうだ。
```

*Apparently he didn't come to yesterday's meeting.*

い-adjectives behave the same way, because an い-adjective's plain form can already finish a sentence by itself. 寒[さむ]い is a complete plain sentence, so 寒[さむ]いそうです is a complete report.

```jp
今年[ことし]の冬[ふゆ]はとても寒[さむ]いそうです。
```

*I hear this winter is going to be very cold.*

Now the part that trips people up in week one. な-adjectives and nouns cannot end a plain sentence on their own — they need だ, the plain version of です (the word that works like *is/am/are*). That だ is part of the plain form, so it does not disappear. It stays, and そうだ goes behind it.

```jp
静[しず]かだ → 静[しず]かだそうだ
```

*it is quiet → I hear it is quiet*

```jp
あの町[まち]は夜[よる]とても静[しず]かだそうです。
```

*I hear that town is very quiet at night.*

Nouns work identically: noun, then だ, then そうだ. If you can say 医[い]者[しゃ]だ as a plain sentence, you can say 医[い]者[しゃ]だそうだ as a report of one.

```jp
彼[かの]女[じょ]のお父[とう]さんは医[い]者[しゃ]だそうです。
```

*I hear her father is a doctor.*

And when the report is about the past, the noun's plain past form だった does the work, with そうだ unchanged behind it as always.

```jp
あの人[ひと]は去[きょ]年[ねん]まで学[がく]生[せい]だったそうです。
```

*I hear that person was a student until last year.*

So the system is: build the sentence plainly, get the tense and the negation right there in front, then attach そうだ. Four shapes, one rule, and three of the four need no thought at all.

## Rules and exceptions

そうだ is a dead end, grammatically speaking. Once you attach it, the sentence is over. It does not take a past form, it does not take a negative form, and it does not politely agree with anything around it.

> そうだ itself never conjugates. `寒いそうでした`, `寒いそうだった` and `寒いそうじゃない` are all wrong, no matter what the sentence is doing.

The reason is worth holding onto, because it makes the rule stop feeling arbitrary. そうだ is not a claim about the world; it is a label stuck on the outside of a sentence saying where that sentence came from. A label has no tense. So if the cold weather is already over, that fact belongs to the adjective, not to the label: 寒[さむ]かったそうです. And if the report is that something is *not* the case, the negation belongs to the verb or adjective in front: 来[こ]なかったそうです.

The one thing that does change is politeness, and only in one place. そうだ is the plain version, そうです the polite one — that is the entire politeness system for this pattern. What you must not do is push the politeness forward into the sentence itself.

> Never attach そうだ to a ます form. `行きますそうです` is wrong even in the most formal conversation you will ever have; it is 行[い]くそうです, with the plain 行[い]く sitting inside the polite ending.

This surprises people, because everywhere else politeness seems to spread. Here it does not, and that is actually the pattern telling you something true: the sentence in front of そうだ is a quotation of what you were told, and quotations keep their own plain shape.

Two more edges. First, hearsay そうだ does not go into questions. `雨が降るそうですか` is not how you ask someone whether they heard about the rain — to ask, you just ask normally and let them answer with そうです. Second, do not use it for anything you experienced yourself. If you stood in the rain this morning, 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]りました is the honest sentence; 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]るそうです says plainly that you are working from someone else's information.

It is also worth knowing what そうだ does *not* do. It is not a hedge. It does not signal that you doubt the report or that you think it is unreliable — it is neutral relay, the same tone a news reader uses. If you want to name where you got it, do that in a separate sentence first (友[とも]達[だち]から聞[き]きました) and then deliver the report. The そうだ sentence itself stays clean.

## Politeness and casual speech

そうだ does not contract, which is unusual — most endings of this size shrink in fast speech. What changes instead is where you meet it. Plain そうだ is completely normal in writing, especially anything news-shaped, and it is what you will see on a page. In polite conversation, そうです is standard and safe.

In casual talk between friends it takes the usual final particles and nothing else: 安[やす]いそうだよ, 寒[さむ]いそうだね. That works, though among close friends そうだ can sound slightly bookish — there are shorter, chattier ways of relaying gossip that you will meet later. Nothing you are learning here becomes wrong; you are just learning the version that is correct everywhere, which is the right order to learn things in.

## Contrast: そうだ against ので and のに

You already know two patterns described with the same three words, *plain form plus*: ので for a neutral reason, のに for "even though". They live in the same slot, they attach to the same forms, and for verbs and い-adjectives all three behave identically. Then you hit a な-adjective or a noun, and they split.

ので and のに take な after a な-adjective or a noun. そうだ takes だ.

```jp
あの町[まち]は静[しず]かなので、私[わたし]は好[す]きです。
```

*That town is quiet, so I like it.*

```jp
あの町[まち]は静[しず]かなのに、私[わたし]はあまり好[す]きじゃありません。
```

*Even though that town is quiet, I don't like it much.*

Put those next to あの町[まち]は夜[よる]とても静[しず]かだそうです and the difference is one syllable: な for ので and のに, だ for そうだ. This one trips up nearly everyone, and the mistake always runs the same direction — `静かなそうです`, borrowed straight from ので habits. If you catch yourself writing な in front of そう, you have merged two patterns.

There is a deeper split underneath the syllable. ので and のに are joints: they connect two halves of a sentence that you are asserting, and something always follows them. そうだ is a lid: it closes the sentence and tells your listener the whole thing came from elsewhere, and nothing follows it. That is why one of them can carry tense inside a longer sentence and the other cannot — a joint is part of the machinery, a lid is not.

There is a second そうだ coming, and it looks identical from the outside. The difference is entirely in what sits in front of it: hearsay needs a complete plain form, while the other one attaches to a bare stem and talks about how something looks to you. So when you meet a そう in the wild, read backwards, not forwards — the shape in front of it is the whole answer.

Build the sentence plainly, then hang そうだ off the end and leave it alone. That is the pattern.
caution_notes: そうだ never conjugates itself — put every tense and negation on the plain form in front of it, never on そうだ.
After a な-adjective or a noun you need だ before そうだ, not the な that ので and のに take.
Attach そうだ only to a plain form, never to a ます form, even when the whole sentence is polite.
Do not use hearsay そうだ for something you saw or experienced yourself; it always points at a source outside you.

items.explanation_markdown:
You are at the window of a shop near the station, looking at a tray of bread that came out of the oven ten minutes ago. You want to say something about it, and you reach for このパンはおいしいです — which is a small lie. おいしい is a verdict from your tongue, and your tongue has been nowhere near that tray. What you actually have is your eyes.

```jp
このパンはおいしそうですね。
```

*That bread looks delicious, doesn't it.*

That is the whole job of this そう. It takes a word about how something **is** and turns it into a word about how something **strikes you right now, from what is in front of you**. It is a guess made on the spot, from visible evidence, and Japanese would rather you marked it as a guess than smuggled it in as fact.

You will need it constantly. Luggage that looks heavy, a friend who looks tired, a sky that is obviously about to do something. All of that runs through そう.

## How it works

One move: **cut the word back to its stem, then put そう on the end.** The stem is the word with its ending taken off — the part that carries the meaning, before the grammar starts.

- い-adjectives drop their い.
- な-adjectives are already stems, so nothing goes between them and そう.
- Verbs go to the ます-stem, the shape you are left holding when you pull ます off the polite form.

```jp
高[たか]い → 高[たか]そうです
元[げん]気[き] → 元[げん]気[き]そうです
降[ふ]る → 降[ふ]りそうです
```

*expensive → looks expensive*

*well → looks well*

*to fall (of rain) → looks about to fall*

Why a stem and not a whole form? Because そう is not standing outside a finished sentence and commenting on it. It fuses onto the word and builds a **new adjective** out of it. 高[たか]そう is a single word meaning "expensive-looking", exactly the way 高[たか]い is a single word meaning "expensive". Hold onto that idea — half of this lesson falls out of it.

な-adjectives are where learners over-engineer things. There is no な, no だ, nothing at all in the gap. 元[げん]気[き] walks straight into そう.

```jp
兄[あに]は今日[きょう]とても元[げん]気[き]そうです。
```

*My older brother looks really well today.*

He has not told you how he feels. You are working from the fact that he is up early and talking. `元気なそうです` is the slip almost everyone makes once, borrowed out of ので habits — but there is nothing to borrow here, because そう attaches to the bare word and to nothing else.

Verbs shift the meaning slightly, and this part catches people. With an adjective, そう tells you how something appears. With a verb, it tells you the action is **on the verge of happening** — you are watching the run-up to it, not the thing itself. 降[ふ]りそう does not mean "rain is a thing that occasionally happens here"; it means "that rain is coming, any minute now". A cat inching toward the edge of a desk is 落[お]ちそう. A train sitting three minutes too long at the platform is 遅[おく]れそう.

```jp
雨[あめ]が降[ふ]りそうなので、傘[かさ]を持[も]ちます。
```

*It looks like it's going to rain, so I'll take an umbrella.*

Notice the そうな in there. That is the second half of the pattern, and you get it for free: **そう behaves exactly like a な-adjective**. Once you have built 高[たか]そう or 降[ふ]りそう, you can do to it everything you already do to 元[げん]気[き] or 静[しず]か. Before a noun it takes な. Before a verb it takes に. In a polite sentence it takes です, and in the past, でした.

```jp
おいしそうなパンを三[みっ]つ買[か]いました。
```

*I bought three delicious-looking rolls.*

```jp
子[こ]供[ども]は楽[たの]しそうに歌[うた]います。
```

*The child sings as though she's having a wonderful time.*

That そうに is the workhorse for describing **how** somebody does something: 楽[たの]しそうに, 悲[かな]しそうに, 忙[いそが]しそうに. You are not claiming to know what is going on inside another person — you are reporting the shape of it from the outside, which is precisely what そう is for.

Tense goes on そう and nowhere else, because そう is the adjective now: 高[たか]そうでした, "it looked expensive". The word in front never moves. 高[たか]い stays 高[こう], whenever the guess was made.

Negatives take a little care, and they split in two. To say something does not look a certain way, you make そう itself negative: 高[たか]そうじゃないです. To say an action does not look about to happen, the ない fuses in front instead, growing a さ on the way: 電[でん]車[しゃ]は遅[おく]れなさそうです.

## Rules and exceptions

Two words are irregular, and both are common enough that you will meet them this week. いい and ない are too short to survive the chop, so they grow a さ first.

> いい becomes よさそう and ない becomes なさそう. `いそう` and `なそう` are wrong. And yes, いい switches to its 良[よ]い root on the way, exactly as it does everywhere else it conjugates.

Then the trap that every learner walks into once.

> `かわいそう` is a real word, and it does **not** mean "cute-looking". It means "poor thing" — pity, not charm. To say a cat looks cute, say かわいい猫[ねこ]ですね and keep そう out of it entirely.

Nouns are simply out of scope. そう builds adjectives out of adjectives and verbs, and a noun has no ending to chop. `学生そうです` is not a sentence in any register. If you want to guess someone's job from their bag, this pattern cannot carry you there — you will need a different tool, and you will get one later.

The last rule is honesty running the other way. そう is for a judgement built from partial evidence. When the fact is just plainly there in front of you, do not hedge it. A room you are standing in the middle of is 静[しず]かです, not `静かそうです`, and something plainly pretty is きれいです, not `きれいそうです`. きれい and かわいい are already verdicts delivered by the eyes, so stacking そう on top of them either sounds strange or, as you just saw, means something else altogether.

## Casual speech

In casual talk the です or だ falls straight off and そう ends the sentence by itself: 高[たか]そう, おいしそう, 安[やす]そう. This is one of the most common things you will hear friends say to each other over a menu. Add a final particle and you have the rest of it — 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]りそうだね, おいしそうだよ. The negative shortens the same way: 高[たか]くなさそう.

Because そう is doing the guessing for you, this ending is safe with strangers as well as with friends. おいしそうですね said to the person who cooked is a compliment, not a hedge — you are telling them their food is winning before you have even started. Nothing needs softening; you only swap です in or out.

## Contrast: the そうだ you were told against the そうだ you can see

You have met そうだ once already, for hearsay, and from the outside the two are identical. They are unrelated patterns, they never mix, and the thing that tells them apart sits **in front** of そう, never behind it.

Hearsay takes a **complete plain form** — something that could stand alone as a sentence. Appearance takes a **bare stem** — a word with its ending cut off. So the minimal pair splits on exactly one い.

```jp
来[らい]週[しゅう]の試[し]験[けん]は難[むずか]しいそうです。
```

*I hear next week's exam is hard.*

```jp
来[らい]週[しゅう]の試[し]験[けん]は難[むずか]しそうです。
```

*Next week's exam looks hard.*

The first sentence is a message from someone who sat that exam last year, and you have no opinion of your own in it. The second is you, holding the study sheet, doing the arithmetic on how much of it you actually know. Same exam, completely different source, one syllable of difference.

な-adjectives split even more visibly, and this is where all three patterns you now know pull apart. ので and のに take な: 静[しず]かなので, 静[しず]かなのに. Hearsay そうだ takes だ: 静[しず]かだそうです. Appearance そう takes nothing whatsoever: 静[しず]かそうです. Three endings, three joints, one stem, and the syllable sitting in the gap tells you which one you are reading. This trips up nearly everyone for a fortnight, and then one day it stops.

There is a deeper difference under the syllable. Hearsay そうだ is a lid: it shuts the sentence and never conjugates. Appearance そう is a word: it takes な, it takes に, it goes past, it goes negative, it happily lives inside a longer sentence. That is why 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]りそうなので works and why the hearsay one could never be bent into that shape.

So read backwards, not forwards. A full form in front means somebody told you. A bare stem in front means you are the one looking.

Later, when you meet たら, this ending becomes one of the most useful things you own — "if it looks like rain, ..." is a sentence people say most weeks of their lives, and you are one small step away from it.
caution_notes: Attach this そう to a bare stem — an い-adjective without its い, a な-adjective with nothing after it, a verb's ます-stem — never to a full plain form and never to a noun.
いい becomes よさそう and ない becomes なさそう; the chopped forms いそう and なそう are wrong.
かわいい plus そう gives かわいそう, which means “poor thing” rather than “cute-looking”.
Unlike the hearsay そうだ, this そう conjugates as a な-adjective: そうな before a noun, そうに before a verb, そうでした in the past.

items.explanation_markdown:
You and a friend have tomorrow planned out: walk to the park, find a bench, eat the lunch you packed the night before. Then you look up. The sky is the colour of wet paper. Your friend wants to know what happens to the plan in that case, and you need a sentence that hangs the whole afternoon on something that has not happened yet.

```jp
明日[あした]雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ったら、公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きません。
```

*If it rains tomorrow, we're not going to the park.*

Nothing has rained. Nothing has been cancelled. All you have done is build a fork in the road: one branch has rain on it, and on that branch there is no park. Setting up that fork is the entire job of たら.

## How it works

The recipe is short enough to feel like a trick. Take the plain past form of a word — the one ending in た — and stick ら on the end. That is the whole pattern.

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べた → 食[た]べたら
飲[の]む → 飲[の]んだ → 飲[の]んだら
```

*eat → ate → if/when (someone) eats*
*drink → drank → if/when (someone) drinks*

Look at the second one for a second. 飲[の]む does not become `飲みたら`; its past tense is 飲[の]んだ, so the conditional — the form that means *supposing this happens* — is 飲[の]んだら. Same story with 泳[およ]ぐ → 泳[およ]いだ → 泳[およ]いだら. That is where the だら you sometimes see listed as a separate form comes from. It is not a second rule to memorise; it is the same ら glued onto a past form that already ended in だ. Get the past tense right and だら takes care of itself.

The irregulars stay boring, which is a genuine relief: する → した → したら, and 来[く]る → 来[き]た → 来[き]たら. No surprises, no extra sounds.

There is a reason this pattern is built on the past form rather than the dictionary form, and it is worth two seconds of your attention. The た form in Japanese is not purely about yesterday — it marks an event as **completed**. たら takes that completed event and says *treat this as done, and now what?* Once you hear it that way, the fact that one pattern covers both *if* and *when* stops being strange. Both of them are just "this is finished — next".

### Adjectives and nouns join in

たら is not a verbs-only club. い-adjectives have a past tense of their own, so they take ら exactly the same way: 安[やす]い → 安[やす]かった → 安[やす]かったら.

```jp
この本[ほん]が安[やす]かったら、買[か]います。
```

*If this book is cheap, I'll buy it.*

な-adjectives and plain nouns lean on だった instead: 暇[ひま] → 暇[ひま]だった → 暇[ひま]だったら, and 雨[あめ] → 雨[あめ]だった → 雨[あめ]だったら. Nothing new to learn there either — if you can make the past tense of a noun sentence, you can make its conditional.

```jp
明日[あした]暇[ひま]だったら、一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ませんか。
```

*If you're free tomorrow, shall we watch a movie together?*

Notice what the second half of that one is doing. It is not a prediction — it is an invitation. たら is perfectly comfortable with a request, an invitation, or a suggestion after the comma. The fork is allowed to end in *let's*, not only in *this will happen*. Hold onto that; it turns out to be one of the main things that separates たら from the other conditionals waiting for you.

Negatives need no new machinery, because every ない form behaves like an い-adjective: 分[わ]からない → 分[わ]からなかった → 分[わ]からなかったら.

One ordering rule, and it does not bend: the たら clause comes first. The condition is the setup, the second half is the payoff, and Japanese will not let you deliver them in the other order.

### When "if" is really "when"

English forces you to choose between *if* and *when*, and the choice leaks information. *If I get home* sounds like there is some chance you won't. Japanese simply refuses to make you decide — たら covers both, and the listener works out which one you meant from how likely the first half is.

```jp
家[いえ]に帰[かえ]ったら、すぐ電[でん]話[わ]します。
```

*When I get home, I'll call you right away.*

Nobody hearing that thinks getting home is in doubt. The first event is a certainty, so たら reads as *once that's done* — a sequence, not a gamble. Same shape as the rain sentence, same grammar, and the only thing that changed is how sure everyone is about the first clause. This one trips people up in the first week, and the fix is not more grammar: it is noticing that Japanese is leaving something to context that English spells out.

### The past-tense version is a different animal

Put the second half into the past tense and たら stops predicting anything at all. Now it reports. You did the first thing, and the second thing was already sitting there waiting for you.

```jp
冷[れい]蔵[ぞう]庫[こ]を開[あ]けたら、猫[ねこ]がいました。
```

*When I opened the fridge, there was a cat.*

You opened a fridge and met a cat. That mixture — one small ordinary action, and then something nobody ordered — is exactly the flavour of past-tense たら. It is how Japanese says *and then, of all things...*, and it shows up constantly in stories about your own day.

## Rules and exceptions

- Build it from the past form, never the dictionary form. `行くら` and `飲みたら` are the two wrong guesses everyone makes, and both come from skipping the past-tense step in the middle.
- The たら half stays plain, always. Politeness is settled once, at the end of the sentence: 電[でん]話[わ]します is polite, 帰[かえ]ったら is not, and the sentence as a whole is polite anyway.
- The たら clause goes first. There is no version of this where you tack the condition on at the end as an afterthought.

> When the second clause is in the past tense, whatever follows たら has to be something that happened *to* you — a discovery, a surprise, a result you did not steer. `冷蔵庫を開けたら、猫を買いました` breaks, because buying is a decision, and you cannot discover your own decision.

> たら is not a machine for translating every English *if*. If the *if* you have in mind is really the reason for something that already happened, you have reached for the wrong tool — that is ので territory, and the two of them are worth seeing side by side.

## Casual speech

たら has no contracted form to learn; it is already about as short as Japanese gets. What it does have is a casual habit — people cut the sentence off right after it and let their voice carry the rest.

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]に聞[き]いたら？
```

*Why don't you ask the teacher?*

Rising intonation, and the missing second half is something like *wouldn't that sort it out*. It is a suggestion, not a question about the past, and every bit of its force lives in the pitch. Say it to a friend and it sounds helpful. Say it to your own boss and it lands somewhere between blunt and nagging, so keep this one for people at your level or below.

## たら against ので and のに

Here is the comparison that makes たら click. The form 降[ふ]った — the past of 降[ふ]る — turns up in all three of these patterns. The only thing that changes is what you hang on the end of it.

```jp
雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ったので、公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きませんでした。
```

*Because it rained, we didn't go to the park.*

```jp
雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ったのに、公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きました。
```

*Even though it rained, we went to the park.*

Both of those are reports from the real world. ので says the rain happened and it was the reason we stayed in. のに says the rain happened and we went anyway, which was mildly ridiculous of us. Neither one leaves any doubt about the weather: it rained, full stop.

Now put the very first sentence of this lesson back next to them. The core is the same 降[ふ]った, but that little ら turns the rain from a fact into a possibility. Nothing has been settled, nobody has stayed home, and the sentence is describing a branch of the future rather than a piece of the past.

So the test is quick. Has it already happened? Then you want ので for the reason, or のに for the contradiction. Has it not happened yet — or has it not happened *so far as you know*? That is where たら lives.

One line to carry away: past form plus ら, and your sentence splits neatly into *this is done* → *then that*. Everything else is just noticing whether the first half is a gamble or a certainty, and trusting context to tell your listener which. Soon you will meet ば and なら, two more ways to say *if* — ば for what is always true, なら for *well, if we're talking about that* — and たら is the one that will carry your conversations comfortably while you sort those two out.
caution_notes: Build たら from the plain past form, not the dictionary form — if the past tense ends in だ, the conditional ends in だら.
Politeness is decided by the final verb only, so the たら clause itself stays plain even inside a polite sentence.
The たら clause always comes first; the condition is the setup and never an afterthought tacked onto the end.
With a past-tense second clause たら reports something you ran into, so it cannot be followed by an action you deliberately chose.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're standing in a shop, staring at a price tag, trying to decide whether to buy something. You already know how to say 高[たか]いです — it's expensive — but what you actually want is a personal rule, something that applies not just today but every time you're in this situation: expensive means no. That's the job of ば. It builds a general-truth "if," the kind that states a standing condition rather than describing one specific moment.

```jp
高[たか]ければ、買[か]いません。
```

*If it's expensive, I won't buy it.*

Think of ば as the Japanese version of the "if X, then Y" you'd write in a rulebook or a recipe, not the "if" you'd use to describe one particular afternoon. Nobody's talking about this one item on this one day — the sentence is a policy you carry around with you, ready for the next price tag and the one after that.

It attaches to the end of whatever sets up the condition, and the shape it takes depends on what kind of word that is — a verb, an adjective, or a noun / な-adjective. Four families, four small changes. None of them are hard once you see the pattern underneath, and you already know every verb and adjective involved; this lesson is really just teaching you one new ending to bolt on.

That's also why ば is worth learning properly instead of skimming: it's the ending you reach for constantly once you start noticing how much of daily talk is really a string of small standing rules — what you do when it's late, what you buy when it's cheap, what happens when a friend calls. English handles all of that with one word, "if." Japanese wants you to first decide whether you're stating a rule or narrating an event, and only then pick the right ending.

## How it works

**Group 1 verbs** — the ones ending in う, く, す, つ, ぬ, ぶ, む, or a る that doesn't behave like an い/え-stem verb — shift their final sound from the u-row to the e-row, then add ば. 話[はな]す (to speak) becomes 話[はな]せば. This is the same row-shift you'll eventually recognize all over the language; here it's just doing conditional duty instead of something else.

```jp
ゆっくり話[はな]せば、分[わ]かります。
```

*If you speak slowly, I'll understand.*

**Group 2 verbs** — ones like 見[み]る or 食[た]べる whose stem already ends in an い or え sound before る — just drop the る and add れば. The irregular 来[く]る follows the same shape, which is one less thing to memorize separately.

```jp
彼[かれ]が来[く]れば、嬉[うれ]しいです。
```

*If he comes, I'll be happy.*

**する**, the other irregular, becomes すれば. Every verb built on する — 勉[べん]強[きょう]する, 練[れん]習[しゅう]する, and every other noun-plus-する verb you've picked up — inherits this same change automatically, so you never have to look it up twice.

```jp
毎[まい]日[にち]練[れん]習[しゅう]すれば、上手[じょうず]になります。
```

*If you practice every day, you'll get good at it.*

**い-adjectives** drop the final い and add ければ. The plain negative ない rides along on this same rule, since grammatically it behaves exactly like an い-adjective — it ends in い, so it conjugates like one.

```jp
忙[いそが]しくなければ、手伝[てつだ]います。
```

*If I'm not busy, I'll help.*

**な-adjectives and nouns** don't take ば directly — there's no verb-like stem for it to grab onto, since these words lean on the copula だ instead of conjugating on their own. Instead, that だ turns into なら, which is casual and by far the most common choice, or into the more formal であれば, which you'll see more in writing and polite speech than in conversation.

```jp
静[しず]かなら、勉[べん]強[きょう]できます。
```

*If it's quiet, I can study.*

```jp
学[がく]生[せい]であれば、安[やす]いです。
```

*If you're a student, it's cheap.*

Look back at those examples and you'll notice ば never actually shows up by itself except right after a verb — せば、れば、すれば、ければ、なら、であれば are all the same idea, just wearing whatever shape the word in front of it demands. Once you can spot the base word hiding underneath the ending, none of these are a surprise anymore; you're not learning six patterns, you're learning one pattern with five outfits.

## Rules and exceptions

Here's the edge that catches almost everyone the first time through: when the ば clause describes an action rather than a state, the sentence can't end in a command, an invitation, or a "let's."

> `図書館に行けば、本を借りましょう` sounds broken to a native ear even though every piece is conjugated correctly. Swap the front clause to たら instead, and it becomes completely natural: 図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]に行[い]ったら、本[ほん]を借[か]りましょう。 ("Once you get to the library, let's borrow a book.")

It helps to have a reason, not just a rule to memorize: ば is stating something like a law of the world — a standing fact about how things work — and a law doesn't turn around and hand out orders in the same breath. たら, by contrast, is just narrating one step and then the next, so a command or invitation fits naturally after it.

That restriction lifts as soon as the front clause is a state instead of an action — an adjective, a negative, or a stative verb like 分[わ]かる. That's exactly why 忙[いそが]しくなければ、手伝[てつだ]います works without a hitch: 忙[いそが]しい isn't an action, it's a description of how things are, and a description doesn't carry the same weight of "law" that an action does.

There's a second trap worth flagging: ければ only ever attaches to the plain form of an adjective. There's no polite version of the ending itself — you build it off 高[たか]い, never off a -です or -ます shape of anything.

A third thing worth knowing: because ば describes a standing rule rather than one moment, it also does the job of a hypothetical — the "if I were, if I had" kind of if, about something that isn't true right now. The mechanics don't change at all; only the situation you're picturing does, and context usually makes clear which one you mean.

## Casual speech

In relaxed speech, ければ often shrinks further, to けりゃ or even きゃ. 高[たか]ければ can turn into 高[たか]けりゃ, and 忙[いそが]しければ into 忙[いそが]しけりゃ. It reads as blunt and a little rough around the edges, the kind of thing you'll hear from an older relative or in a casual drama more than from a coworker — worth recognizing when you hear it, not something you need to produce yet.

## Contrast: ば vs. たら

You already know たら for conditionals — Ta-form + ら. The two overlap enough on the surface to blur together, and honestly, in a lot of everyday sentences either one gets the point across and a native speaker won't blink. But they're answering different questions underneath. ば states a standing rule, something generally or always true; たら describes one specific event, usually something you're picturing as a single occurrence, often already decided by the time you're saying it.

```jp
雨[あめ]が降[ふ]れば、家[いえ]にいます。
```

*If it rains, I stay home.*

```jp
雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ったら、家[いえ]にいます。
```

*If it rains, I'll stay home.*

The English barely shifts, but the Japanese is telling two different stories. The first is a habit — rain, any rain, any day, and you're staying in, full stop, as a rule about yourself. The second is about one forecast, one day: if it rains today, that's what you'll do today, and tomorrow is a separate question. When you're talking about a single, particular event, たら is almost always the safer and more natural pick; save ば for the rule.

ので and のに aren't in this competition at all — they answer "why" and "even though," not "if" — so they don't overlap with ば the way たら does. It's easy to lump every because-shaped or if-shaped word together in your head early on, especially while all of them are still new; this is a good moment to let them separate back out into their own lanes.

You've actually already used なら twice above, quietly doing ば's job for nouns and な-adjectives. That's not the whole of what なら can do, though. On its own as a grammar point, なら can react to something someone just said, or raise a topic before you've even confirmed it's true — a job ば can't touch, since ば always states a rule rather than responding to the moment. Keep today's なら as one shape ば wears; the fuller version of it is still ahead of you.
caution_notes: Don't end a ば sentence with a command, invitation, or "let's" when the ば clause is a plain action verb — use たら there instead.
ければ only attaches to the plain form of an い-adjective (or the plain negative), never to a -です or -ます shape.
Use ば for a standing rule or general truth, not for one specific, already-decided event — that's what たら is for.
であれば and なら are the noun / な-adjective versions of ば; today's なら is not the same grammar point as the topic-based なら you'll meet later.

Your friend corners you after class and says 日本[にほん]語[ご]を勉[べん]強[きょう]したいです — she wants to learn Japanese, and she's asking where to start. You already know exactly the book that got you through your first six months. This is the exact moment なら was built for: not a warning about some hypothetical future, the way English "if" so often is, but a direct reaction to the one thing she just put on the table.

Think about what actually happened in that exchange. She didn't hand you a condition to evaluate — she handed you a topic. Nothing in her sentence was uncertain to her; she wants to study Japanese, full stop. What's open is your response to that topic, and that's exactly the gap なら fills. English blurs this by using "if" for both jobs — real uncertainty ("if it rains") and simple topic-picking ("if it's Japanese you're after, try this book"). Japanese keeps a separate word for the second job, and this is it.

```jp
日本[にほん]語[ご]を勉[べん]強[きょう]したいです。
```

*I want to study Japanese.*

You answer with 日本[にほん]語[ご]なら、この本[ほん]がいいですよ。 Not "if you were to study Japanese, this book would be good" in some abstract sense — closer to "Japanese? Then this book." She names the topic, and なら lets you pick it straight up and react to it.

```jp
日本[にほん]語[ご]なら、この本[ほん]がいいですよ。
```

*If it's Japanese, this book is good.*

That's the whole shape of なら: someone puts an idea on the table — in words, or just by the situation you're both standing in — and なら is how you respond to that specific thing, not to conditions in general.

## How it works

日本[にほん]語[ご] in that sentence is a plain noun, and なら drops right onto it — no extra word in between, nothing to conjugate. That's the easiest case: **Noun + なら**. Whatever sits right before なら is the thing being reacted to, and everything after it is your answer to that one thing.

You already have an instinct for part of this. は marks a plain topic — 日本[にほん]語[ご]は難[むずか]しいです says something true about Japanese in general. なら is what happens when that same topic-picking impulse turns conditional: instead of stating a fact about the topic, you're reacting to the topic having been raised at all. Same instinct, different job.

Verbs work the same way, just in their plain dictionary form. If your friend mentions a plan and you want to react to it directly:

```jp
行[い]くなら、切[きっ]符[ぷ]を買[か]いましょう。
```

*If you're going, let's buy the ticket.*

Nothing gets conjugated there — 行[い]く sits exactly as you'd find it in a dictionary, and なら just follows it.

な-adjectives are the one spot people trip on. Their plain form ends in だ (静[しず]かだ — it's quiet), but なら doesn't want that だ at all — it replaces it:

```jp
静[しず]かだ → 静[しず]かなら
```

*quiet → if it's quiet*

Drop the だ, attach なら directly. Skip that step and you get the very natural-looking but wrong `静かだなら` — an extra だ that shouldn't be there.

```jp
静[しず]かなら、ここで勉[べん]強[きょう]できます。
```

*If it's quiet, you can study here.*

い-adjectives don't have that problem. Their plain form already ends in い, so なら just tacks on with nothing to remove:

```jp
忙[いそが]しいなら、手伝[てつだ]いましょうか。
```

*If you're busy, shall I help?*

And なら isn't stuck reacting to the present moment only. Past tense works too — た-form plus なら reacts to something that, as far as you know, already happened:

```jp
行[い]ったなら、写[しゃ]真[しん]を見[み]せてください。
```

*If you already went, show me the photos.*

Notice the shape holds steady across all of these: whatever form the premise takes — noun, い-adjective, な-adjective (だ dropped), plain verb, or ta-form — なら sits right after it, unchanged itself. All the flexibility lives in what comes before it.

## Rules and exceptions

Here's the part that's easy to get backwards. なら doesn't describe two events happening in order — first this occurs, then that occurs. It reacts to a premise, and that reaction can even land *before* the thing in the なら clause has actually happened. Telling your friend 日本[にほん]に行[い]くなら、カメラが要[い]りますね before she's booked a single ticket is completely normal — you're not narrating a future sequence, you're commenting on a topic she raised, right now.

```jp
日本[にほん]に行[い]くなら、カメラが要[い]りますね。
```

*If you're going to Japan, you'll need a camera.*

> Even the negative version works the same way — 行[い]かないなら (if you're not going) reacts to the same kind of stated premise, not to a future event that fails to occur. なら doesn't care whether the thing actually happens; it only cares that it was raised.

Where people usually reach for なら and get it wrong is when they actually mean "and then" — one action leading straight into the next as a timeline. That's not なら's job. Hold that thought; it's exactly where the contrast section below picks up.

There's also a very natural register this pattern lives in: giving advice or a recommendation on the spot, right after someone tells you something. Native speakers reach for なら constantly in exactly that moment — a friend mentions a plan, a problem, a preference, and なら is how you hand back a suggestion that's clearly tied to what they just said, rather than a generic piece of advice floating free of the conversation.

## Casual speech

In relaxed conversation, plain-form + なら often tightens into んなら. That ん used to be の — the little word that turns a whole idea into "the thing where…" so you can treat it as a single unit and react to it — worn down by fast, casual speech into ん. 行[い]くのなら becomes 行[い]くんなら, and it usually carries a slightly more personal, "oh, since that's how it is" flavor than the plain version.

```jp
行[い]くんなら、僕[ぼく]も行[い]きたいです。
```

*If you're going, I want to go too.*

You'll hear んなら constantly between friends and almost never in writing or anything polite — keep plain なら for anything formal, and save んなら for conversation. If you've noticed わからない shrink into わかんない in the same kind of relaxed speech, this is the same instinct at work: a longer, more explanatory shape wearing down into something quicker once both people already know what's being talked about.

## Contrast

You already have three other conditional-shaped tools, and なら doesn't compete with them so much as sit in its own lane.

たら describes a sequence: this happens, and then that follows. Compare your ticket-buying line from earlier with this one:

```jp
日本[にほん]に行[い]ったら、写[しゃ]真[しん]を送[おく]ります。
```

*When I go to Japan, I'll send photos.*

That's a straight timeline — arrival first, photo-sending after, in that order. Swap in なら for the same sentence and it stops being a timeline entirely; it turns into a reaction to the fact that Japan is even on the table as a topic, with no promise about what happens first.

ば behaves more like a general-truth switch than a reaction to something said. It describes conditions and results with less regard for who mentioned what to whom — it's built for patterns that hold true in general, not for responding to a specific thing your friend just told you. なら, by contrast, only makes sense once something has actually been raised. You can't なら a fact nobody put on the table.

ので is a different animal altogether — it explains a reason, not a condition. 忙[いそが]しいので手伝[てつだ]いません tells you *why* something is true: because you're busy, you won't help. 忙[いそが]しいなら手伝[てつだ]います tells you what you'll do *if* that turns out to be the situation. Reason versus reaction — the two can look similar on the page, but don't let that fool you; swapping one for the other changes what the sentence is actually claiming.

Line them all up against the same friend mentioning she's busy this week, and the differences stop being abstract. たら would describe her getting busy and then something following from it, in that order. ば would describe busyness as a general condition with a general result, no particular friend required. ので would explain busyness as the reason behind something else that's true. なら is the only one of the four that's actually built to react to her having said it — which is exactly why it's the one you reach for most often in ordinary conversation.

The test for なら, every time, is simple: did someone just put something on the table — a plan, a fact, a topic? If so, なら is how you pick it up and answer it directly. Once you meet the can-do form later on, you'll find it pairing with なら constantly — whether something's even possible is just one more thing worth reacting to.
caution_notes: なら reacts to something already said or already known — it is not for two events happening one after another in time, which is たら's job.
な-adjectives and nouns drop だ before なら — 静かだなら keeps an extra だ that does not belong there.
んなら is a casual contraction of のなら used in conversation — avoid it in polite or written Japanese.
Past tense + なら still reacts to a stated premise; it does not turn the sentence into a strict before-and-after sequence.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend wants to go to the beach this weekend, and already has the whole day sketched out — towels, a cooler, maybe a nap on the sand afterward. Before anyone agrees to any of it, there's one practical question standing between you and actually getting in the water.

```jp
泳[およ]げる？
```

*Can you swim?*

That ending isn't a new verb — it's 泳[およ]ぐ (to swim) wearing a different outfit. Japanese has a whole conjugation dedicated to exactly this idea: not "I swim" but "I'm capable of swimming, if it comes to that." It's called the potential form, and once you can build it, you can ask and answer this kind of question about almost anything you already know how to do — not just what you're doing, but what's within your reach to do.

泳[およ]ぐ on its own just states an action: someone swims, or is swimming, or will swim. 泳[およ]げる doesn't state an action at all — it states a standing fact about you, true whether or not you ever actually get in the water this weekend. That's the whole difference between the plain form and the potential form: one reports what happens, the other reports what's possible.

## How it works

The potential form replaces the ending of a verb with れる or られる, attached to the stem — everything before that final る. Which ending you use, and how much of the verb survives the swap, depends on which of three families the verb belongs to. You've already been sorting verbs into these families without necessarily naming them; this is just the first time the split actually changes which ending you reach for.

Ichidan verbs — the ones whose dictionary form always ends in an e-sound or i-sound plus る, like 食[た]べる or 見[み]る — are the easy case. Drop that final る and add られる, and you're done. 見[み]る becomes 見[み]られる, 起[お]きる becomes 起[お]きられる, and the pattern never wobbles.

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べられる
```

*to eat -> can eat*

So if the food at your friend's place turns out fierier than expected, you can still hold your own, and say so without changing anything else about the sentence.

```jp
辛[から]い料[りょう]理[り]も食[た]べられる。
```

*I can even eat spicy food.*

Godan verbs — the ones like 買[か]う or 話[はな]す whose ending actually shifts shape depending on what follows it — do this differently, and it's worth slowing down for. The final u-sound moves back to an e-sound, and る attaches directly, with no られる involved at all. 書[か]く becomes 書[か]ける, 飲[の]む becomes 飲[の]める, and 買[か]う (to buy) becomes 買[か]える.

```jp
買[か]う → 買[か]える
```

*to buy -> can buy*

Same shift, any object you can name.

```jp
傘[かさ]が買[か]える。
```

*I can buy an umbrella.*

This is also why 話[はな]せる already sits in your vocabulary as "can speak" — it was never a separate word to memorize in the first place. It's 話[はな]す run through this exact same shift, and once you see it that way, a handful of other "-eru" words you already know will start looking less like arbitrary vocabulary and more like verbs you'd already half-learned.

The two irregular verbs go their own way, and neither borrows the regular ichidan or godan pattern. する becomes できる, not `すれる` — an irregular jump you've probably already met as its own vocabulary word, long before you needed the grammar behind it. 来[く]る becomes 来[こ]られる, borrowing the ichidan ending even though 来[く]る itself isn't ichidan.

```jp
来[く]る → 来[こ]られる
```

*to come -> can come*

Which means when your friend circles back with the actual invitation, the grammar is already sitting in your hands, fully built.

```jp
週[しゅう]末[まつ]、来[こ]られる？
```

*Can you come this weekend?*

## Rules and exceptions

One habit worth building early: potential-form sentences usually mark what you're able to do with が, not を. 日本[にほん]語[ご]が話[はな]せる, not `日本語を話せる` — you'll hear the second version in relaxed speech, and older textbooks sometimes treat it as acceptable too, but が is the one to default to until you have a feel for when the looser version fits. Some speakers reach for を when the sentence already has a strong sense of "doing something to this specific thing," but that's a nuance to notice later, not a reason to second-guess が now.

> Two words you already know look like they might be potential forms of verbs you've met, and neither one is. 見[み]える ("to be visible") is not the potential of 見[み]る — that would be 見[み]られる. 聞[き]こえる ("to be audible") is not the potential of 聞[き]く — that would be 聞[き]ける. Both describe something reaching you on its own, not your ability to perceive it, and mixing them up is one of the most common slips at this level, precisely because the two pairs look like they should line up and don't.

できる is worth one more note. It started life as する's potential form, but it's drifted into being the everyday word for "possible" or "can," used on its own the way English uses *can* — you'll see it standing alone in sentences that have nothing to do with する at all. That's a normal fate for a potential form popular enough to become a vocabulary word in its own right — it happened to a handful of others too, which is exactly why 話[はな]せる was already sitting in your list before this lesson.

One more thing worth knowing before you go further: once you've built a potential form, it behaves exactly like a brand-new ichidan verb from that point on. 食[た]べられる conjugates like 食[た]べる's cousin, not like the original 食[た]べる — so every negative, past tense, or conditional you build on top of it follows ichidan rules, regardless of which family the original verb came from. That detail is what makes the contrast section below work at all. It also means the negative follows the same ichidan pattern: 食[た]べられる's negative is 食[た]べられない, built the same way you'd negate 見[み]られる or any other ichidan verb, with nothing extra to learn.

## Casual speech

In relaxed conversation, ichidan potential forms routinely drop a syllable in the middle. 食[た]べられる becomes 食[た]べれる — the ら quietly disappears, and nobody blinks.

```jp
食[た]べられる → 食[た]べれる
```

*can eat -> can eat (casual)*

> This dropping only touches ichidan potential forms — the ones built with られる in the first place. Godan forms like 買[か]える or 泳[およ]げる never had a ら to lose, so there's no shortcut to take there. Formal writing and most tests still expect the full られる, and some listeners quietly judge the short version, so treat it as something to recognize on sight before you lean on it yourself.

## Contrast: なら and たら with a potential verb

Once a verb sits in potential form, you'll find it slotting into conditionals you already know — and which one you pick still changes the sentence, even though the potential half stays identical. なら reacts to something already on the table: someone hands you a fact, and なら responds to it directly, almost like the second half of a conversation someone else started.

```jp
日本[にほん]語[ご]が話[はな]せるなら、便[べん]利[り]だ。
```

*If you can speak Japanese, that's convenient.*

Swap in たら, and the sentence stops reacting to a given fact and starts describing a future checkpoint instead — first this becomes true, then that follows, in that order.

```jp
日本[にほん]語[ご]が話[はな]せたら、旅[りょ]行[こう]が楽[たの]しい。
```

*Once you can speak Japanese, travel gets fun.*

Say the なら version and you sound like you're responding to someone who just told you they can speak Japanese. Say the たら version and you sound like you're picturing a future where that's true and imagining what comes after. Same potential verb, same conditional-sounding grammar, genuinely different scene in the listener's head.

The shape doesn't change here — れる and られる will look exactly the same whether the topic is ability or, soon, something being done to you instead of by you. There's no shortcut for telling them apart except context: who's doing what to whom, and whether the sentence is describing a capability or an event landing on someone. Hold onto that; passive voice borrows this exact conjugation next, and sorting the two apart is the hurdle waiting right after this one.
caution_notes: Potential-form sentences usually mark the thing you can do with が, not を — 日本語が話せる is the default, even though the を version shows up in casual speech.
見える and 聞こえる are their own vocabulary words, not the potential forms of 見る and 聞く, which are actually 見られる and 聞ける.
Casual speech often drops the ら from ichidan potential forms (食べられる → 食べれる), but formal writing and most tests still expect the full form.
する's potential form is the irregular できる, not すれる.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your teacher hands back your essay with a note in the margin, and later you're telling a friend how it went. In English you'd probably say "my teacher praised me" — but Japanese has an instinct that flips the sentence around, putting you in the position of receiving the action instead of your teacher in the position of giving it.

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]に褒[ほ]められました。
```

*I was praised by my teacher.*

That's the passive: something happens to the subject of the sentence, and whoever's doing it gets marked with に instead of standing at the front as the subject. Once you can build れる・られる, you can talk about getting complimented, getting your things borrowed, even getting rained on — every situation where you're on the receiving end rather than the one acting. English usually needs "was" plus a past participle to do this; Japanese does it with one verb ending.

## How it works

The passive attaches to the verb stem, and which stem you use depends on the verb's group — the same three-way split you already learned for the potential form. The idea behind all three groups is the same: take the verb, shift it into a stem that no longer commits to a subject deciding to act, and let れる or られる mark that something simply occurred, with you or someone else on the receiving end.

### Ichidan verbs

Drop the final る and add られる.

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べられる
```

*to eat → to be eaten*

```jp
弟[おとうと]にパンを食[た]べられた。
```

*My bread got eaten by my little brother.*

Notice something odd there: パン still has を on it, exactly the marker it would carry in the plain sentence 弟[おとうと]がパンを食[た]べた (my brother ate the bread). The passive didn't promote パン to subject — it just layered "and this happened to me" on top of the original sentence. Hold onto that; it matters again in a minute.

Once you notice the shape, you'll see it everywhere: 見[み]られる (to be seen), 教[おし]えられる (to be taught), 忘[わす]れられる (to be forgotten) are all the exact same stem+られる move, no extra mechanics required.

### Godan verbs

Take the verb's final う-row sound, shift it back one row to あ, and add れる.

```jp
読[よ]む → 読[よ]まれる
```

*to read → to be read*

```jp
手[て]紙[がみ]が読[よ]まれた。
```

*The letter was read.*

This one has no に anywhere — nobody's named as the reader. That's normal for a godan passive describing an event rather than a grievance: the letter got read, full stop, and who did the reading isn't the point.

Verbs ending in う are the one spot where this shift looks strange, because う doesn't have a matching あ-row sound to fall back on — it borrows わ instead.

```jp
使[つか]う → 使[つか]われる
```

*to use → to be used*

You've actually met this あ-row shift before: it's the same vowel step you use to build the negative. 読[よ]む becomes 読[よ]まない the same way it becomes 読[よ]まれる — once you can build one, the muscle memory for the other is already there. The same pattern covers 話[はな]す → 話[はな]される and 呼[よ]ぶ → 呼[よ]ばれる without anything new to learn.

### Irregular verbs

する and 来[く]る don't follow either pattern; you just have to know them.

```jp
する → される
```

*to do → to be done*

```jp
来[く]る → 来[こ]られる
```

*to come → to have someone come*

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]に来[こ]られた。
```

*A friend came over on me, and it was inconvenient.*

That last one is the strangest sentence in this lesson if you translate it word for word, because English won't let you passivize "come" — nobody "gets come to." Japanese doesn't care. れる・られる isn't reserved for things being done to an object; it can mark that an event, even one nobody aimed at you, landed on you and cost you something.

> The passive on an intransitive verb like 来[く]る or 降[ふ]る almost always signals mild inconvenience. 友[とも]達[だち]に来[こ]られた reads less like "a friend visited" and more like "I got visited on, and it threw off my evening."

## Rules and exceptions

に marks whoever performed the action — the teacher who praised you, the brother who ate your bread. Drop it and the sentence becomes a plain, agentless description of something happening, exactly what 手[て]紙[がみ]が読[よ]まれた is doing. You'll drop it constantly: most passive sentences you'll actually use skip the agent, because either it's obvious from context or naming it would sound oddly pointed, almost like an accusation.

The を you saw stay put in 弟[おとうと]にパンを食[た]べられた is a real exception, not a typo. When the passive expresses something being done to your belongings rather than to you directly, the item keeps its を and you keep your ordinary subject slot (an implied 私[わたし]は here). Force the item into が instead — `パンが食べられた` — and you get a completely different, agentless sentence about bread going missing, not about your brother's crime.

> For ichidan verbs and for 来[く]る, the passive and the potential share the exact same conjugation. 食[た]べられる can mean "gets eaten" or "can eat" depending on nothing the verb itself tells you — only the sentence around it decides.

Don't reach for れる・られる just because an English sentence happens to be passive. "The window was broken" usually sounds more natural in Japanese as an active or plain statement unless you specifically need to flag that someone was affected by it — this pattern exists for when being affected is the whole point.

That's also why the passive shows up so often around family and friends rather than strangers and objects: 弟[おとうと]にパンを食[た]べられた only makes sense as a sentence because your bread going missing is *your* problem, not an abstract fact about the world. Compare that to 手[て]紙[がみ]が読[よ]まれた, where nobody's inconvenience is on the table — just an event, reported plainly.

## Contrast: passive vs. potential

You already know れる・られる as the potential form, and the shape really is identical — which is exactly why context has to do the work the verb itself can't. There's a reason the two share a form: both describe the subject *not* being the one driving the action — either the action simply becomes possible on its own, or it simply happens to someone. English treats those as two unrelated grammar categories; Japanese never bothered to split them.

```jp
これは食[た]べられる？
```

*Can this be eaten?*

Nothing here is happening to anyone; nobody's marked with に, and the whole sentence is asking about a quality of これ rather than reporting an event. That's the tell: potential sentences ask about ability or possibility and rarely carry an agent acting on someone, while passive sentences almost always have — or clearly imply — someone whose action lands on someone else.

You'll also hear ら-less shortcuts like `食べれる` in casual speech. That belongs to the potential only — dropping ら is never done for the passive, so 食[た]べられる keeps its full form no matter how casual the conversation gets.

So the real question with any れる・られる sentence isn't just "can I build this," it's "what's actually happening to whom." Keep that question in mind and the two readings stop colliding — you'll find yourself scanning for an agent and a に before you even finish reading the sentence.

This shape isn't done evolving, either. Fuse it with the causative later and you get せられる・させられる, the "made to do it against your will" pattern, which takes exactly the inconvenience you just met in 友[とも]達[だち]に来[こ]られた and turns the volume all the way up.
caution_notes: The passive can attach to intransitive verbs like 来る and 降る to show an event landed on you against your will, and this 'adversity' reading has no direct English equivalent, so avoid translating it word for word.
For ichidan verbs and 来る, the passive form is identical to the potential form — only the surrounding context tells you which meaning is intended.
When the passive describes something happening to your belongings rather than to you, the item can stay marked with を instead of becoming the subject with が — don't rewrite it to が.
Not every English passive sentence should become れる・られる in Japanese; use it only when someone being affected by the action is actually the point.
