items.explanation_markdown:
Your little brother is staring at a plate of vegetables like it personally insulted him. You've tried asking nicely. You've tried bargaining. Tonight you're done negotiating — he's going to eat them, whether he likes it or not. English hands you one verb, "make," and expects tone of voice to do the rest. Japanese hands you a whole new verb form built for exactly this moment.

That form is the causative — a version of the verb that puts *you* in charge of someone else's action instead of describing your own. Where 食[た]べる means "eat," 食[た]べさせる means "make (someone) eat" — or, in gentler situations, "let (someone) eat." Same ending, two very different dinners.

```jp
母[はは]は弟[おとうと]に野[や]菜[さい]を食[た]べさせる。
```

*Mother makes her little brother eat vegetables.*

You'll hear this shape constantly from whoever gets to call the shots in a given relationship — parents, teachers, doctors, bosses. It isn't rude on its own; it's just the grammar of someone directing someone else's action, the way "have someone do something" works in English. Whether the mood underneath is a stern order or a small kindness is a separate question, one you'll unpack a little further down.

## How it works

The causative attaches to the same verb stem you already know from potential and passive — you're not learning a new attachment point, just a new thing to attach.

For an ichidan verb (the ones ending in an -eru or -iru you can just drop), knock off る and add させる:

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べさせる
```

*to eat → to make (someone) eat*

For a godan verb, shift the final syllable back from the "u" row to the "a" row, then add せる — the exact same vowel shift you already did for potential and passive, just with a different auxiliary bolted on:

```jp
行[い]く → 行[い]かせる
```

*to go → to make (someone) go*

The two irregulars don't follow either pattern, so they're just worth memorizing outright:

```jp
する → させる
```

*to do → to make (someone) do*

```jp
来[く]る → 来[き]させる
```

*to come → to make (someone) come*

> 来[き]させる looks like plain 来[く]る with させる stuck on, but the reading underneath shifts — 来[く]る is くる, while 来[き]させる is こさせる. It's the same quirk you've already met in 来[こ]ない (こない); the kanji stays put, the reading moves.

Once you've built the causative verb, it behaves like any other verb ending in -eru — it takes ます, ない, た, all the endings you already use every day. 食[た]べさせます, 食[た]べさせない, 食[た]べさせた. Nothing new to learn there.

That する rule pays off well beyond the bare verb "to do." Every noun-plus-する verb you know — 掃[そう]除[じ]する, 勉[べん]強[きょう]する, 練[れん]習[しゅう]する — swaps its する for させる the exact same way: 掃[そう]除[じ]させる, 勉[べん]強[きょう]させる, 練[れん]習[しゅう]させる. You've already memorized dozens of these nouns; you're not adding new vocabulary, just reusing the one irregular conjugation across all of them.

The one genuinely new decision is which particle marks the person being made to act. It depends on whether the verb is *transitive* — one that takes a direct object, like 食[た]べる (eat *something*) — or *intransitive*, one that doesn't, like 走[はし]る (run). With a transitive verb, the object keeps its を and the person doing the acting gets に, same as sentence one above: 弟[おとうと]に野[や]菜[さい]を. With an intransitive verb, there's no object competing for を, so the person takes it instead.

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]は学[がく]生[せい]を走[はし]らせる。
```

*The teacher makes the students run.*

```jp
私[わたし]は弟[おとうと]に薬[くすり]を飲[の]ませる。
```

*I make my little brother drink the medicine.*

Notice 走[はし]る has nobody else to give を to, so 学[がく]生[せい] takes it. 飲[の]む already has 薬[くすり] sitting on を, so 弟[おとうと] gets に instead. Once you see the object competing for the particle, the split stops feeling arbitrary — check whether the verb already needs a を, and hand the leftover particle to whoever's being made to act.

This scales to any verb you already know without extra memorizing. 話[はな]す has an object (you speak *something*), so its causee takes に. 泳[およ]ぐ doesn't, so its causee takes を. You're not learning a new fact per verb — you're just asking the one question you already know how to answer from ordinary sentences: does this verb take an object or not?

## Rules and exceptions

Nothing in the grammar itself tells you whether a causative sentence is bossy or generous — that's entirely down to context. The same structure that forces your brother to eat vegetables can just as easily describe a parent being soft.

```jp
母[はは]は子[こ]供[ども]を公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]ばせる。
```

*Mother lets her child play in the park.*

Nobody has to twist a child's arm to get them into a park. Swap the scene to homework and the identical grammar reads as strict instead of kind — the sentence doesn't change; your mental picture of the situation does.

> The single most common slip is dropping the さ on an ichidan verb — writing `食べせる` instead of 食[た]べさせる. Ichidan causatives are always -させる, never a bare -せる; the shorter form only happens on godan verbs, where せる is already doing all the work after the vowel shift.

The causee particle rule has no exceptions worth worrying about, but it does have one boundary worth stating outright: whatever the verb, the person being made or allowed to act is never marked with が. That particle stays reserved for the thing someone wants, likes, or is capable of — categories that belong to entirely different patterns, not this one. If you find が creeping into a causative sentence, you've drifted into potential without meaning to.

Because the causative puts you above someone else in the sentence, it can land harshly if you aim it at a superior — a boss, a teacher, someone older. Softening that is a matter of surrounding vocabulary and tone rather than a rule the grammar itself enforces, so for now, just notice that the bare causative describes *who's directing whom*, not how anyone involved feels about it.

## Contrast

You've actually met れる・られる twice already — once for potential, once for passive — and both times it attached to the same stem you're using now. せる・させる sits right next to them structurally, which is exactly why it's easy to blur the three together under pressure. The fix is remembering who the sentence is about: potential and passive both put the subject on the receiving end of the verb; causative puts the subject in the driver's seat, making the action happen *to* someone else.

```jp
弟[おとうと]は野[や]菜[さい]が食[た]べられる。
```

*My little brother can eat vegetables.*

食[た]べられる and 食[た]べさせる are one vowel apart and mean almost opposite things — one says he's capable of it, the other says somebody's forcing the issue. When you catch yourself unsure which one you meant, ask who's actually chewing. If it's the subject of the sentence, you want potential. If the subject is pulling strings from outside the action, you want causative. Notice, too, that 野[や]菜[さい] sits on が in the potential sentence and on を in the causative one — the particle swap you just learned to spot for causees works as a quiet tell for which pattern you're looking at.

The same test travels to any verb pair you already know. Take 走[はし]らせる from earlier: swap さ for れ and you'd be saying the student is capable of running, 走[はし]れる, not that anyone ordered him onto the track. The vowel is the whole difference between an ability and an instruction.

Sometimes the two even stack: someone gets made to do something, and *they're* the one stuck experiencing it rather than causing it. That flip side — being on the receiving end of somebody else's causative — gets its own form soon: せられる・させられる, the causative-passive. Today's job is just getting comfortable putting other people in the driver's seat you're steering from. The version where somebody else steers *you* can wait.
caution_notes: Mixing up causative せる／させる with potential／passive れる・られる produces a real but wrong-meaning verb, so always check who is actually performing the action.
Ichidan verbs always take させる, never a bare せる — writing 食べせる instead of 食べさせる is the single most common slip.
Whether a causative sentence reads as forceful or permissive is decided entirely by context, not by the grammar itself.
The causee's particle depends on whether the verb is transitive (に) or intransitive (を), and it is never marked with が.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend tops up your glass. You already said you were done, you meant it, and the glass is full again anyway. The next morning someone asks how the night went, and none of the sentences you own quite fit. 私[わたし]は飲[の]む is true, but it makes the whole evening sound like your project. A sentence with your friend as the subject puts the spotlight on them, when the story is really about what happened to you.

This is the sentence you want:

```jp
私[わたし]は友[とも]達[だち]にお酒[さけ]を飲[の]まされる。
```

*My friend makes me drink.*

飲[の]まされる is two forms you already have, welded together. You know 飲[の]ませる, the causative — the make-or-let form. You know 飲[の]まれる, the passive — the form where the action lands on you rather than starting from you. Stack the passive on top of the causative and you get the form for sitting on the wrong end of somebody else's decision: they decided, your body carried it out, and you would rather it hadn't.

That last part is not decoration. This pattern is not neutral, the way English "I was asked to" is neutral. Built into it is the fact that you didn't want to. A speaker who chooses this form is complaining — mildly, maybe fondly, but complaining.

## How it works

Two moves, always in this order: build the causative first, then make that causative passive.

Start with a る-verb (ichidan — the ones that simply drop る). 食[た]べる goes to causative 食[た]べさせる, and then the せる ending swaps to せられる.

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べさせられる
```

*to eat → to be made to eat*

Put it to work on the child who has strong opinions about dinner:

```jp
弟[おとうと]は毎[まい]晩[ばん]野[や]菜[さい]を食[た]べさせられる。
```

*Every night my little brother is made to eat his vegetables.*

う-verbs (godan) take the same two steps, plus a shortcut the language worked out for you a long time ago. 飲[の]む goes to 飲[の]ませる, and that goes to 飲[の]ませられる. Four syllables of ending is a lot to carry, so せられ got squeezed down to され.

```jp
飲[の]む → 飲[の]ませられる → 飲[の]まされる
```

*to drink → to be made to drink (long form) → to be made to drink (short form)*

Both are correct Japanese. The long 飲[の]ませられる is what the textbook builds and what you meet in careful writing; the short 飲[の]まされる is what people actually say, and it is the one that will come flying at you in conversation. Recognize both. Produce whichever one you can assemble faster under pressure — nobody will mark you down.

The two irregular verbs behave themselves. する becomes させられる and 来[く]る becomes 来[き]させられる. Every する-verb inherits this automatically, so 掃[そう]除[じ]する gives 掃[そう]除[じ]させられる, 勉[べん]強[きょう]する gives 勉[べん]強[きょう]させられる, and so on down the list.

```jp
私[わたし]は日[にち]曜[よう]日[ひ]に掃[そう]除[じ]させられる。
```

*On Sundays I get put to work cleaning.*

Now the particles, which you can borrow wholesale from the passive. The person who made it happen takes に — the friend with the bottle, the teacher with the worksheet. The thing the action lands on keeps を. And you, the one whose hands and mouth actually did the unwanted thing, are the topic or subject: は or が.

The shape, then, is: victim は instigator に object を verb.

## Rules and exceptions

The short form has one hard limit: it belongs to う-verbs only, and only to those that don't end in す. 話[はな]す builds its causative as 話[はなし]させる, so the causative-passive is 話[はな]させられる. Contracting that would hand you `話さされる`, with さ crashing into さ, and Japanese simply refuses.

```jp
私[わたし]は会[かい]議[ぎ]で英[えい]語[ご]を話[はな]させられる。
```

*At meetings I'm the one who gets made to speak English.*

> Never contract an ichidan verb either. `食べさされる` is not a form. る-verbs and す-verbs use the long ending, full stop.

待[ま]つ deserves its own line, because 待[ま]たされる is one of the highest-frequency members of this entire family. Waiting is the classic thing that gets done to a person.

```jp
私[わたし]は駅[えき]で一[いち]時[じ]間[かん]待[ま]たされる。
```

*I get left waiting at the station for an hour.*

Notice how the English drifts there. "Made to wait" is stiff; "kept waiting" is what an English speaker actually says. Expect that. The Japanese form is one consistent thing, but the natural English for it changes verb by verb, and chasing a single English formula will make your translations worse, not better.

> される on its own is also the plain passive of する. So 掃[そう]除[じ]される means something got cleaned — nobody was forced into anything. If you mean a person was put to work, you need the extra syllable: 掃[そう]除[じ]させられる.

One more edge, and this one is social rather than mechanical. Because the pattern carries a complaint, you don't use it for things you chose, even unpleasant ones. Stayed late for 残[ざん]業[ぎょう] because you decided the work needed finishing? Plain sentence. Stayed late because the office kept you there? The causative-passive is exactly right, and everyone hearing it will pick up the resentment without you adding a single extra word.

## Casual speech

The contraction above *is* casual speech doing its work, and in conversation it goes further: the plain forms crowd out the polite ones. Among friends you'll hear 飲[の]まされる and 飲[の]まされた far more often than 飲[の]ませられます, and the long 飲[の]ませられた can land as slightly formal, or as someone deliberately slowing down to make a point of it.

For ichidan and す-verbs there's no shortcut available, so casual speech just strips the politeness instead: 食[た]べさせられた, 話[はな]させられた, 掃[そう]除[じ]させられた. The ending stays long because it has nowhere shorter to go.

## Contrast

Here is the minimal triple. Same two people, same beer, three grammars, three completely different stories.

First, the causative you already know. Your older brother is the one making decisions:

```jp
兄[あに]は私[わたし]にビールを飲[の]ませる。
```

*My older brother makes me drink beer.*

Now the plain passive. Same brother, but nobody is forcing anybody — the beer was yours, he drank it, and the sentence exists because you're annoyed:

```jp
私[わたし]は兄[あに]にビールを飲[の]まれる。
```

*My brother goes and drinks my beer on me.*

And the causative-passive, where you are the subject just like in the passive, but this time the beer went down your throat:

```jp
私[わたし]は兄[あに]にビールを飲[の]まされる。
```

*My brother makes me drink beer.*

Hold the first and the third side by side. They report one single event from two different seats. 兄[あに] has the plan in both of them; what changes is who the sentence is about and whose experience we're being told. Swap them by accident and you've just claimed to be the one pouring.

There's a bonus here, and it's rare enough to be worth pointing out. 食[た]べられる has to work three jobs at once — passive, potential, and polite — and you disambiguate it from context. 食[た]べさせられる has no such problem. However long it is, it means exactly one thing, every time. The length is the price of the clarity.

## A closing thought

Causative plus passive, in that order, with に on whoever is responsible and you as the topic — and a built-in shrug of complaint that you can't switch off. Keep half an eye on the fact that being made to do something for long enough tends to end somewhere else entirely: there's a pattern coming, ようになる, for the moment a thing you couldn't do becomes a thing you just do.
caution_notes: The shortened ending belongs only to う-verbs that do not end in す; ichidan verbs and す-verbs keep the long ending.
話す gives 話させられる and never `話さされる`, because two さ in a row is blocked.
される alone is also the plain passive of する, so 掃除される means something got cleaned while 掃除させられる means a person got put to work.
The person responsible is marked with に, and the form always carries a note of complaint — if the choice was yours, use a plain sentence instead.

items.explanation_markdown:
You've taped a note to the fridge door and you're halfway through writing it when you remember who's going to read it: a six-year-old. So you start over and make the letters twice as big.

Nothing about *what* you wrote changed. What changed is the reason behind how you wrote it — and that reason isn't a word, it's a whole little sentence: *so that the kid can read it*. Japanese hangs that sentence in front of the main one and glues it on with ように.

```jp
子[こ]供[ども]にも読[よ]めるように、大[おお]きく書[か]きました。
```

*I wrote it big so that even a child could read it.*

読[よ]める is the potential form you already know — *can read*. Everything before ように is the situation you're aiming at. Everything after it is what you actually did to get there. The comma is doing real work: it's the seam between goal and action.

## How it works

ように attaches to a plain, non-past verb. That's two options: dictionary form (読[よ]める, 聞[き]こえる, 分[わ]かる) when you want something to happen, or ない form (遅[おく]れない, 忘[わす]れない, 入[はい]らない) when you want something *not* to happen. Then a comma, then the thing you did or will do.

The negative version is at least as common as the positive one, and it's usually the first one learners actually need — most of daily life is arranging things so a small disaster doesn't occur.

```jp
電[でん]車[しゃ]に遅[おく]れないように、早[はや]く家[いえ]を出[で]ました。
```

*I left home early so that I wouldn't be late for the train.*

Look at 遅[おく]れない. It's plain, even though the sentence ends politely with 出[で]ました. That's not sloppiness — it's the rule. More on that in a moment.

Now the part that decides whether your sentences sound native or slightly off: **the verb in front of ように is normally something nobody directly controls.** Potential forms live here happily (読[よ]める, 聞[き]こえる, 見[み]える, できる, 分[わ]かる), and so do intransitive verbs — verbs that describe something simply happening rather than someone doing it to something (入[はい]る, 遅[おく]れる, 止[と]まる, 無[な]くなる).

```jp
みんなに聞[き]こえるように、大[おお]きい声[こえ]で話[はな]しました。
```

*I spoke in a loud voice so that everyone could hear.*

聞[き]こえる is *to be audible* — you can't order someone's ears to work. You can only adjust your voice and hope. That gap between "what I can do" and "what I want to come about" is exactly the space ように fills.

That also means the two halves of the sentence often have **different subjects**, which surprises people the first time.

```jp
猫[ねこ]が入[はい]らないように、窓[まど]を閉[し]めます。
```

*I'll close the window so that the cat doesn't get in.*

The cat is the one entering; you're the one closing. Two people (well, one person and one cat) in one sentence, and Japanese doesn't mind at all. This is typical, not an edge case.

```jp
犬[いぬ]が水[みず]を飲[の]めるように、皿[さら]を庭[にわ]に置[お]きました。
```

*I put a dish in the garden so the dog could drink water.*

Same shape: dog drinks, you place. Potential form before ように, deliberate action after it.

And when the subject *is* the same on both sides, the verb before ように is still something outside your direct command:

```jp
忘[わす]れないように、ノートに書[か]きます。
```

*I write it in my notebook so I won't forget.*

You can't decide to remember. You can only decide to write. That's the whole logic of the pattern in one sentence.

## Rules and exceptions

**Never put a past-tense verb in front of ように when you mean purpose.** Not because it's ungrammatical, but because it quietly turns into something else. 忘[わす]れたように means *as if he'd forgotten* — a comparison, not a goal. So `忘れたように、ノートに書きます` doesn't say what you think it says.

**Politeness lives at the end of the sentence, never before ように.** `読めますように、大きく書きました` is wrong mid-sentence. The clause before ように is always plain; the final verb carries the politeness for the whole thing.

> There is one place where ますように is not only fine but standard: at the very end of a sentence, alone, as a wish. It's a fossil — a leftover shape that survived because people kept saying it. See the casual section below.

The most common wrong guess is putting a **fully controllable action** before ように. Something like `日本語を勉強するように、毎日ノートに書きます` sounds strange, because studying is a thing you simply decide to do — there's no gap for ように to bridge. The fix is usually to reach for the potential form and describe the *state* you want instead: 日本[にほん]語[ご]が分[わ]かるように. Rule of thumb: if you could stick "I'll just decide to" in front of the verb and it still makes sense, ように is the wrong tool. Japanese has a separate pattern for deliberate-action goals, and you'll meet it later.

> Watch out for ように after a noun plus の. 猫[ねこ]のように歩[ある]く means *to walk like a cat* — that's a comparison, a completely different animal that happens to share a spelling. Purpose ように always sits on a verb.

## Casual speech

Here's the good news: ように is one of the rare patterns that doesn't contract, shorten, or shift at all. 忘[わす]れないように is 忘[わす]れないように in a boardroom and in a group chat. What changes is only the *end* of the sentence — 忘[わす]れないように、ノートに書[か]きます becomes 忘[わす]れないように、ノートに書[か]く, and that's the whole difference.

The one form worth memorizing on its own is the standalone wish, which keeps ます even among friends:

```jp
明日[あした]雨[あめ]が降[ふ]りませんように。
```

*Please, let it not rain tomorrow.*

No main clause, no comma, nothing after it. You'll hear this at shrines, before exams, and muttered at the sky by anyone who left the laundry out.

## Contrast

You already know ば, and it can look deceptively close, because both patterns pair up two events.

```jp
早[はや]く出[で]れば、電[でん]車[しゃ]に遅[おく]れません。
```

*If you leave early, you won't be late for the train.*

Compare that with 電[でん]車[しゃ]に遅[おく]れないように、早[はや]く家[いえ]を出[で]ました from earlier. ば puts the condition first and the automatic consequence second: leave early → not late, as a general truth. ように flips the emotional order. The goal comes first because the goal came first *in your head*, and the second clause is the choice you made because of it. ば describes how the world works; ように describes why you did something.

The causative せる・させる is worth a second look too, because both patterns are about making things happen.

```jp
子[こ]供[ども]に薬[くすり]を飲[の]ませました。
```

*I made the child take the medicine.*

```jp
子[こ]供[ども]が一人[ひとり]で飲[の]めるように、薬[くすり]を水[みず]に入[い]れました。
```

*I put the medicine in water so the child could drink it alone.*

The causative applies force to a person: I acted on you, you did the thing. ように applies force to *the situation*: I rearranged the world until the thing became possible, and then it happened on its own. One is a push, the other is clearing the path.

So: goal in front, action behind, plain non-past verb at the seam, and something you can't directly control sitting before ように. That last condition is the one to keep hold of — because when the thing that was impossible finally *does* become possible, Japanese has a pattern built out of this exact よう, and you'll want to see it coming.
caution_notes: The verb before ように must be plain and non-past — politeness belongs only to the final verb of the sentence.
A past-tense verb before ように stops meaning purpose and starts meaning 'as if'.
Put something outside your direct control before ように — a potential form or an intransitive verb — not a fully deliberate action.
Noun + のように is a comparison meaning 'like', not a purpose; purpose ように always attaches to a verb.

items.explanation_markdown:
You've been going to the pool every weekend since spring, and this morning you crossed the whole thing without stopping once. A friend asks how it's going. You could say 泳[およ]げます — it's true, and it's flat. It reports today and says nothing about the four months of not being able to do it. What you actually want is the word for the *arrival*.

```jp
私[わたし]は泳[およ]げるようになりました。
```

*I've become able to swim.*

That's ようになる. It takes a verb and says: this wasn't happening before, and now it is. The whole pattern is about the line you crossed, not about where you're standing.

## How it works

The machinery is small. Take a verb in plain dictionary form, add よう, then attach なる — the same なる you already use for 寒[さむ]くなる and 上手[じょうず]になる. よう by itself means something like *way* or *manner*, so the literal shape is "it becomes the way where you swim." That's clumsy English but a useful picture: the situation reshapes itself around the verb.

There are two flavours, and which one you get depends entirely on what you put in front of よう.

**Potential form + ようになる** is new ability. You couldn't, now you can. This is why the pattern shows up constantly in language-learning talk.

```jp
漢[かん]字[じ]が少[すこ]し読[よ]めるようになりました。
```

*I've become able to read a little kanji.*

読[よ]める is the potential form you already know; ようになりました is what turns a static ability into a story with a before and an after.

**Dictionary form + ようになる** is a new habit or tendency. Nobody gained a skill here — the behaviour simply started happening where it didn't used to.

```jp
弟[おとうと]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]早[はや]く起[お]きるようになった。
```

*My younger brother has come to get up early every morning.*

He could always get up early. He just didn't. 毎[まい]朝[あさ] is doing a lot of work in that sentence — habit words like 毎[まい]日[にち], 毎[まい]晩[ばん], よく and いつも sit very naturally with this flavour, because a habit needs repetition to be visible.

The subject doesn't have to be a person, and the change doesn't have to be anyone's project:

```jp
猫[ねこ]が私[わたし]のベッドで寝[ね]るようになりました。
```

*The cat has taken to sleeping on my bed.*

Now the tail. なる is an ordinary う-verb, so it conjugates normally and carries the whole tense and politeness load for the sentence: ようになります, ようになりました, ようになった, ようになって. In practice you'll write the past form more than anything else, because you usually notice a change after it's finished happening. ようになります points at a change you expect later — after this course, after the operation, after next month.

```jp
一人[ひとり]で電[でん]車[しゃ]に乗[の]れるようになりましたか。
```

*Have you become able to ride the train by yourself?*

For the negative — the verb *stops* happening — you can build 〜ないようになる, and it's grammatical:

```jp
父[ちち]はコーヒーを飲[の]まないようになりました。
```

*My father has stopped drinking coffee.*

Hold that one loosely, though. It's the form the textbook shows, and it's not what most people say out loud. More on that at the end.

## Rules and exceptions

The first sharp edge is the one everyone hits: **choosing the wrong flavour**. If you mean an ability and you write the dictionary form, you've said something different but perfectly grammatical, so nothing warns you. `泳ぐようになりました` means you started swimming — took it up, go regularly now. 泳[およ]げるようになりました means you couldn't and now you can. Two true sentences about the same summer, and only one of them is your sentence.

> Verbs that already carry a potential meaning inside them don't take a potential form first. 分[わ]かる, できる, 見[み]える and 聞[き]こえる go straight in: 分[わ]かるようになりました, できるようになりました. `分かれるようになる` is a form you'll be tempted to build once and should never build again.

The second edge is **politeness placement**. Everything before よう stays plain, always. `泳げますようになりました` is wrong in a way that sounds jarring to a native ear — です and ます can't live in the middle of the sentence like that. Put the politeness on なる, where it belongs, and leave the front end alone.

Third: this is a pattern about **change over time, not a single event**. A verb under ようになる should be repeatable or continuous. "I came to arrive at the station at 8:15 yesterday" isn't a thing anyone says in any language, and it isn't a thing ようになる can express either. If the event happened once, on one day, you want a plain past tense and nothing more.

Fourth, and this is where the pattern is genuinely mushy: ようになる leans towards changes that happened **to** you rather than changes you announced. Ability arriving after months of practice, a habit that crept in, a cat that made a decision. It's not a rule you can violate and get an error — plenty of native sentences use it for deliberate changes — but the default colour of the word is gradual and slightly outside your control, which is why だんだん sits so comfortably in front of it.

On casual speech there's less to say than you might expect: ようになる doesn't contract. What changes is the tail you already know how to change — ようになりました becomes ようになった, and that's the whole story. You'll occasionally hear the よう squeezed almost to nothing in fast speech, but there's no separate casual form to learn.

## Contrast

The closest thing you already know is ように, and the two are one syllable apart for a reason — they're the same よう, pointing in opposite directions in time. ように is the **goal you're aiming at**; ようになる is the **goal you reached**.

```jp
泳[およ]げるように毎[まい]日[にち]練[れん]習[しゅう]します。
```

*I practise every day so that I'll be able to swim.*

That's ように: the swimming hasn't happened yet, it's the reason for the practice. Swap the tail and the practice disappears from the sentence entirely, replaced by its outcome — 泳[およ]げるようになりました. If you find yourself unsure which you want, ask whether the verb in front of よう has actually happened. Not yet, and it's the point of some other effort? ように. Already true, and it wasn't before? ようになる.

The second comparison is with the bare potential form on its own. 泳[およ]げます is a **state**: true today, no claim about last year. 泳[およ]げるようになりました is an **event**: the moment the state switched on. This is why answering どうですか about your Japanese with 話[はな]せるようになりました is warmer than 話[はな]せます — you've told the person there was a struggle.

One last piece of housekeeping. You already say 上手[じょうず]になる and 元[げん]気[き]になる without any よう, and you might reasonably wonder why verbs need the extra part. 日本[にほん]語[ご]が上手[じょうず]になりました — *I've gotten good at Japanese* — is exactly that: no よう anywhere. Adjectives and nouns can attach to なる directly, because なる wants a description of a resulting state and that's exactly what they are. A verb isn't a description — it's an action — so よう does the conversion, packaging "swim" into "the state of things where swimming happens." Same なる, one extra bridge.

So: ようになる marks the switch flipping, potential form in front for a new ability, dictionary form for a new habit. And that negative you're holding loosely — 飲[の]まないようになりました — is about to get a shorter, much more natural rival when we meet なくなる, which does the same job in fewer syllables and is what your father would actually say about the coffee.
caution_notes: Potential form before ようになる means a new ability; plain dictionary form means a new habit, and both sentences are grammatical, so nothing will flag the wrong choice.
Verbs that already mean 'can' — 分かる, できる, 見える, 聞こえる — attach directly, never in a potential form.
Keep everything before よう plain; ます and です belong on なる at the end of the sentence.
Use it for changes that repeat or continue over time, not for a single completed event.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your older brother used to have coffee in his hand from morning until night. Lately, every time you see him, it is water. You want to say this in Japanese, and the first thing that comes to mind is 飲[の]みません — but that just says he does not drink coffee, flat and timeless, as if the man had never touched the stuff in his life.

What you actually mean has a shape to it. There was a before, there is an after, and somewhere in between the coffee quietly stopped. Japanese has a pattern for exactly that shape.

```jp
兄[あに]はコーヒーを飲[の]まなくなりました。
```

*My older brother stopped drinking coffee.*

Two moving parts: a negative, and a becoming. Someone became a person who does not do the thing. That is the entire idea, and once you see it that way the form almost builds itself.

## How it works

Start from the verb's ない form — the plain negative you already make every day. Then remember something you may not have been told out loud: ない behaves like an い-adjective (a describing word ending in い, like 高[たか]い or 寒[さむ]い). And you already know what happens to an い-adjective in front of なる — the い becomes く.

So 飲[の]まない loses its い, becomes 飲[の]まなく, and takes なる on the end.

```jp
飲[の]む → 飲[の]まない → 飲[の]まなくなる
する → しない → しなくなる
来[く]る → 来[こ]ない → 来[こ]なくなる
```

*drink → does not drink → comes to no longer drink*
*do → does not do → comes to no longer do*
*come → does not come → comes to no longer come*

The two irregular verbs behave themselves here, which is a small mercy. する and 来[く]る just hand over their normal negative stems and the rest is mechanical.

Notice where the politeness sits. The first verb stays plain forever — it is buried inside the pattern, not at the end of the sentence — and all the tense and politeness work happens on なる: なる, なります, なりました, なった. If you want the polite past, you get 〜なくなりました, and nothing else in the sentence changes.

The pattern is about change, so it loves subjects that drift. A cat, for example, who has decided that the food it demanded for three years is now beneath it.

```jp
猫[ねこ]が魚[さかな]を食[た]べなくなりました。
```

*The cat stopped eating fish.*

It also works beautifully for things that fade out of your reach rather than things you decide about. Rain comes down, the air goes white, and the mountain that was there a minute ago is simply not available to your eyes anymore.

```jp
雨[あめ]で山[やま]が見[み]えなくなりました。
```

*Because of the rain, the mountain became impossible to see.*

That sentence is worth sitting with, because English wants two different words here — *stopped* for the cat, *became impossible* for the mountain — and Japanese uses one. The pattern does not care whether a person chose the change. It only reports that the state flipped from doing to not doing.

And it flips for the inside of your head too. Names, meanings, whole trains of thought can go the same way as the mountain.

```jp
彼[かれ]の名[な]前[まえ]が分[わ]からなくなりました。
```

*I no longer know his name.*

One more piece of range: because ない is an い-adjective, the pattern is not limited to verbs. Any negative that ends in ない can take the same treatment, so 寒[さむ]くない becomes 寒[さむ]くなくなる — the nights stopped being cold. You will meet this less often than the verb version, but when you meet it, it is the same machine.

## Rules and exceptions

The first trap is a spelling one, and it catches almost everyone once. The ない must lose its い. Writing `飲まないなる` or `飲まないになる` feels reasonable — なる takes に after nouns, after all — but ない is not a noun here, it is a describing word, so it goes to 飲[の]まなく and takes なる bare.

The second trap is politeness creeping to the wrong end of the sentence. `飲みませんなる` is not a thing. Politeness is a coat you put on last, and here the last word is なる.

> ある has no negative form of its own — its negative simply *is* ない. So ある plus this pattern collapses into なくなる with nothing in front of it, which is spelled exactly like the ordinary verb 無[な]くなる (to run out, to disappear). お金[かね]がなくなりました is the ordinary verb, and everyone reads it that way. That overlap is not a bug you can fix; it is just how the two words landed on top of each other, and context does the sorting.

The third thing is less a rule than a warning about meaning. This pattern describes a change that has settled in, not a single refusal at a single moment. If your brother turns down one cup of coffee on one Tuesday, that is not 飲[の]まなくなりました — that is just him saying no today. The pattern claims that the world is different now than it was.

> Because it reports a change rather than a decision, なくなる carries no intention at all. 学[がっ]校[こう]に来[こ]なくなりました says a person stopped showing up; it says nothing whatsoever about whether they meant to, and a listener will not assume they did.

The pattern is also perfectly happy in the plain non-past, 〜なくなる, when you are talking about something that has not happened yet — the coffee will stop, the mountain will disappear. Learners tend to lock onto 〜なくなりました because that is where they first met it, but the future half of the pattern is just as real.

## Casual speech

In conversation the ending drops its politeness and you get 〜なくなった, which is by far the form you will actually hear. Beyond that, the contractions you already know keep working inside the pattern, because the first half is just a normal negative doing normal negative things.

```jp
分[わ]からなくなった → わかんなくなった
```

*stopped understanding → stopped getting it (casual)*

That わかんない for 分[わ]からない is the same casual squeeze you have met before, and it survives the trip into this pattern intact. It is friends-and-family speech only — say it to a teacher and it will land oddly.

## Contrast

You already know ようになる, which is this pattern's mirror twin. ようになる is the door opening: someone reaches the point of doing a thing, or becomes able to. なくなる is the door closing.

```jp
兄[あに]はコーヒーを飲[の]むようになりました。
```

*My older brother started drinking coffee.*

Put that beside the sentence you opened this lesson with and the only difference is the direction of travel. Same brother, same coffee, same なる underneath, opposite arrows. If you can build one, you can build the other, and it is worth deliberately practising them as a pair.

The sharper contrast is with the potential form れる・られる, because that is where a real meaning difference hides. Compare 漢[かん]字[じ]を読[よ]まなくなりました with this:

```jp
漢[かん]字[じ]が読[よ]めなくなりました。
```

*I became unable to read kanji.*

The first one — 読[よ]まなくなりました — says you can still read kanji perfectly well, you just do not anymore. The books are on the shelf and you walk past them. The second one, with the potential 読[よ]める inside, says the ability itself went away: you sit down with the page and nothing comes. Same pattern, and the entire difference in your life is whether れる・られる is in there.

This is one of the places where Japanese is more precise than English, which cheerfully uses "stopped reading" for both. When you build a sentence, ask yourself which one you mean, because your listener will hear the answer.

One last neighbour worth naming: 見[み]える and 聞[き]こえる are already about things arriving at your senses on their own, so 見[み]えなくなる is the natural way to say something slipped out of sight, and you do not need the potential form on top of it.

## A closing thought

Negative, then becoming: the state flipped from doing to not doing, and the sentence reports the flip without judging it. Hold onto how neatly this pattern pairs with ようになる — you are about to meet はず, and the moment you can say what someone has stopped doing, you will want to say what they were supposed to be doing instead.
caution_notes: The ない must lose its い before なる — 飲まなくなる, never 飲まないなる or 飲まないになる.
All tense and politeness go on なる at the end; the verb inside the pattern stays plain.
なくなる reports a settled change over time, not a single refusal on a single occasion, and it carries no sense that the person intended it.
Since ある's negative is ない, ある plus this pattern collapses into なくなる, which looks exactly like the ordinary verb 無くなる (to run out).

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend messaged twenty minutes ago to say they were getting on the train. The ride takes fifteen minutes. Now someone turns to you and asks where they are. You cannot say 彼[かれ]は駅[えき]にいます — that is a flat claim about the world, and you have not seen anything with your own eyes. But you are not guessing at random either. You have a departure time and a train that takes fifteen minutes, and those two facts point somewhere.

```jp
彼[かれ]はもう駅[えき]にいるはずです。
```

*He should be at the station by now.*

That is the job はず does. You park a whole plain-form clause in front of it and it says: from what I know, this is how things must be. Not a hope, not a shrug — you have grounds, and the grounds are doing the talking.

## How it works

はず is a formal noun — a word shaped like a noun that never stands on its own, existing only so that a clause can be attached in front of it. That single fact explains almost every rule below, so it is worth holding onto.

Two consequences follow. Whatever comes *in front* of はず connects the way it would connect to any ordinary noun. Whatever comes *after* はず is just ordinary noun endings: だ when plain, です when polite, でした or だった in the past.

Verbs are the easy case. A dictionary-form verb attaches to nouns without help, so it attaches to はず without help:

```jp
電[でん]車[しゃ]は八[はち]時[じ]に出[で]るはずです。
```

*The train is supposed to leave at eight.*

Notice there is no guessing in that sentence. It is the timetable speaking through you. This is the natural home of はず: schedules, arrangements, arithmetic, anything where a fact you already have implies a fact you do not have yet.

Tense goes on the verb, not on はず. If the thing you are reasoning about already happened, the verb carries the past and はず stays exactly as it is:

```jp
母[はは]は昨日[きのう]この手[て]紙[がみ]を出[だ]したはずです。
```

*My mother should have sent this letter yesterday.*

English smears the past across the whole phrase there — *should have sent* — which is why learners reach for something like `出すはずでした` when they mean this. Resist it. Past on the verb means the event is expected to have happened; past on はず means something else entirely, and we will get to it in a moment.

Negatives behave the same way. Negate the clause, leave はず alone:

```jp
彼[かの]女[じょ]は今日[きょう]の会[かい]議[ぎ]に来[こ]ないはずだ。
```

*She is not due to come to today's meeting.*

い-adjectives also attach bare, since they already modify nouns with no connector:

```jp
この店[みせ]のコーヒーは安[やす]いはずです。
```

*The coffee at this shop should be cheap.*

Now the two forms that trip everyone up in the first week — and it really is everyone, so do not take it personally. な-adjectives keep their な. It is the same な you already use in 静[しず]かな部屋[へや]; はず is noun-shaped, so it wants the same treatment a noun would get:

```jp
夜[よる]の図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]は静[しず]かなはずだ。
```

*The library at night should be quiet.*

And a plain noun needs の to hook onto はず, exactly as one noun needs の to modify another:

```jp
あの人[ひと]は医[い]者[しゃ]のはずです。
```

*That person should be a doctor.*

> `静かはず` and `医者はず` are the two most common wrong guesses in this pattern. If you can remember that はず is a noun in disguise, you can rebuild both rules from scratch instead of memorising them.

Because the ending is ordinary, you can put はず itself into the past — and that is where the meaning shifts:

```jp
私[わたし]たちは先[せん]週[しゅう]旅[りょ]行[こう]するはずでした。
```

*We were supposed to travel last week.*

> Past-tense はず almost always means the expectation *failed*. はずでした and its plain twin はずだった say: this was the arrangement, and it did not happen. A Japanese speaker hearing 旅[りょ]行[こう]するはずでした will immediately want to know what went wrong.

## Rules and exceptions

The first sharp edge is the English word *should* itself. In English it does two unrelated jobs: it calculates (*the train should be here by now*) and it instructs (*you should call your mother*). はず only ever does the first one. It has nothing to say about duty, advice, or what a decent person would do. If you tell a friend 電[でん]話[わ]するはずです, you have not urged them to call — you have announced that, as far as you understand the schedule, a call is going to occur.

The second edge follows from the first. Be careful using はず about your own actions. 私[わたし]は明日[あした]行[い]くはずです is not wrong, but it means your going is fixed by something outside you: a booking, a rota, somebody else's plan. If *you* are the one who decided, say 行[い]きます. Using はず about your own free choice makes you sound strangely detached from your own life, like you are reading your day off a printout.

Third: はず needs grounds. There has to be a reason sitting behind the sentence, even an unspoken one. If you have no reason and you are simply guessing, 多[た]分[ぶん] is the honest word. And the two are not rivals — 多[た]分[ぶん] is an adverb, so it can sit inside a はず sentence when your grounds are real but thin.

Fourth, a small mercy: politeness lives entirely on the ending. はずだ is plain, はずです is polite, and nothing about the clause in front has to change. You can build the whole sentence casually and then decide at the last syllable how formal you are being.

## Casual speech

In relaxed speech the だ falls off and はず ends the sentence bare. This is extremely common — arguably more common than the full form when you are talking to a friend:

```jp
鍵[かぎ]はかばんの中[なか]にあるはず。
```

*The key should be in the bag.*

Said with a slight rise, that bare はず carries a faint *I think, anyway* — the speaker is inviting you to check. Adding よ (あるはずだよ) pushes the other way and sounds more certain, like you are settling a small argument. でしょ in place of だ (あるはずでしょ) drags the listener in and asks them to agree with you.

All three are the same grammar with different social weather. The clause in front never moves.

## Contrast

The closest thing you already know is ようになる, and holding the two side by side sharpens both. ようになる reports a change you have actually observed landing — it asserts that the world is now this way:

```jp
妹[いもうと]は日本[にほん]語[ご]が話[はな]せるようになった。
```

*My little sister has got to the point where she can speak Japanese.*

Say that and you are claiming to have heard her do it. Swap in はず and you get 妹[いもうと]は日本[にほん]語[ご]が話[はな]せるはずだ, which is a different speech act altogether: you have not heard her, but you know she has been studying for two years, so you are computing the result. ようになる is a report. はず is an inference.

なくなる splits the same way. 彼[かれ]はもうお酒[さけ]を飲[の]まなくなった says the drinking stopped and you watched it stop. 彼[かれ]はもうお酒[さけ]を飲[の]まないはずだ says you have some reason to believe he does not drink any more — his doctor, something he told you last month — but you are reconstructing, not reporting. Both sentences can be true at once; only one of them is a claim you would defend if challenged.

The test is simple. If someone said *how do you know?*, could you answer *I saw it*? Then you do not want はず. If your answer would be *well, because…* followed by a reason, はず is the word.

So: はず is not a soft guess and not a piece of advice. It is you doing arithmetic out loud on the facts you already hold, with な after な-adjectives and の after nouns, and with the past tense meaning very different things depending on whether it lands on the verb or on はず itself. Hold onto that last part — when we meet はずがない shortly, you will find it does not merely negate this pattern, it flips it into something much more forceful.
caution_notes: な-adjectives keep their な and plain nouns take の before はず — 静かなはず and 医者のはず, never 静かはず or 医者はず.
はず never gives advice or states an obligation; it only says what you calculate to be true from the facts you have.
Put past tense on the verb when the event is expected to have happened — past tense on はず itself means the expectation failed.
Avoid はず about your own free decisions; it implies your action is fixed by an outside arrangement rather than by you.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend swears he already finished his homework. You know better — you were sitting right next to him for the last two hours, and he never once put down the remote. He watched TV, laughed at something on screen, got up for a snack, came back, and sat right back down. Not once did he open his backpack, let alone take out a pencil.

So when he tells you the homework is done, you don't quietly doubt him or ask a polite follow-up question. You don't need to ask him to prove it, either — you already have all the proof you need, sitting right there in what you watched happen. You say it flat out, because you were there and you know what you saw.

```jp
彼[かれ]が宿[しゅく]題[だい]をしたはずがない。
```

*There's no way he did his homework.*

This is はずがない — *there's no way / can't be*. It doesn't hedge the way *maybe he didn't* would, and it isn't the same as a plain *he didn't*. It rules the thing out entirely, as a conclusion, and it can only do that because you have something concrete standing behind it: two hours of watching him do everything except homework.

You already know はず for the opposite job — something you're confident will turn out to be true. 彼[かれ]が来[く]るはずだ, *he should be coming*, says you expect something to happen based on what you know. はずがない takes that same word and closes the door on it completely: はず (the case that should hold) plus が plus ない (doesn't exist) — literally *there is no case in which that's true*. Put the pieces together and you get the strongest, flattest way Japanese has to say something is impossible. And exactly like はず, it never floats free — there's always a reason behind it, even when the speaker doesn't bother to say it out loud.

## How it works

はずがない attaches to a plain-form predicate the exact same way はず does. That's good news: you're not learning a new attachment rule from scratch, you're just adding が plus ない to the end of a shape you already build correctly.

A plain verb — dictionary form, ta-form, whatever tense the sentence needs — slots straight in, no extra piece required.

```jp
彼[かれ]が今日[きょう]休[やす]むはずがない。
```

*There's no way he's taking today off.*

He's got an exam this afternoon — 試[し]験[けん]があるから — and skipping the one day that actually matters simply isn't something he'd do. The reasoning is doing all the work here; the sentence itself is just the conclusion.

An i-adjective works the same way: plain form, nothing added before はずがない, same as any plain-form sentence you'd already build with it.

```jp
この時計[とけい]が安[やす]いはずがない。
```

*There's no way this watch is cheap.*

You know that one because he bought it at a well-known shop — 有[ゆう]名[めい]な店[みせ]で買[か]ったから — and shops like that don't sell cheap watches. Notice that nothing about 安[やす]い changes; it stays exactly as it would in any other plain sentence.

A na-adjective needs its な first, exactly like it does in front of any noun — that's the one place はずがない asks for something extra, and it's the same extra piece はず already asks for.

```jp
この家[いえ]が便[べん]利[り]なはずがない。
```

*There's no way this house is convenient.*

The reason is sitting right there in the neighborhood — it's far from the station, 駅[えき]から遠[とお]いから — so *convenient* doesn't add up, whatever the listing says.

And a noun takes の, the same の that connects any two nouns in a row.

```jp
彼[かれ]が学[がく]生[せい]のはずがない。
```

*There's no way he's a student.*

He's already got a job — もう会[かい]社[しゃ]員[いん]だから — so *student* doesn't fit anymore, whatever his backpack might suggest.

Four different word types, one shared ending, one job every time: taking something someone claims and flatly ruling it out because the evidence you're holding says it can't be true.

## Rules and exceptions

はずがない isn't for ordinary doubt. If you just personally don't buy something, plain negation or 〜と思[おも]わない carries that weight fine. はずがない is reserved for things you can actually rule out — something you watched happen, a fact you know for certain, a conclusion you can walk someone else through step by step. Say it about a hunch with nothing behind it, and it comes out sounding like you're slamming your hand on the table over something that doesn't deserve it. A listener's next move, fairly, is to ask what makes you so sure — and if the honest answer is nothing, はずがない was the wrong tool from the start.

It's also a stronger, different claim than just negating the verb. 宿[しゅく]題[だい]をしていない simply reports a fact — he hasn't done the homework, full stop, no reasoning attached. 宿[しゅく]題[だい]をしたはずがない makes a claim about reality itself: that the very idea of him having done it doesn't hold up, before anyone even opens the backpack to check. One is an observation; the other is an argument.

> Watch what happens when the thing being denied is already negative. `ないはずがない` — a ない-form verb or adjective plus はずがない — doesn't mean *there's no way that's not true* as a passing, throwaway remark. It flips all the way around into *there's absolutely no way it isn't true*, which lands as *it definitely must be true*.

```jp
彼[かれ]が分[わ]からないはずがない。
```

*There's no way he doesn't understand.*

Read that as *he must understand*, not as some weaker cousin of *he doesn't understand*. Two negatives here don't cancel into something neutral — they cancel into a strong positive claim, which is exactly the trap this pattern sets for anyone translating word by word.

はずがありません is simply the polite dress for the same sentence — same certainty, same reasoning underneath, just appropriate for a teacher, a coworker, or a stranger instead of a friend on the couch next to you.

```jp
彼[かれ]が宿[しゅく]題[だい]をしたはずがありません。
```

*There's no way he did his homework.*

## Casual speech

In fast everyday speech, people commonly drop the が entirely.

```jp
そんなはずがない → そんなはずない
```

Both versions mean exactly the same thing — *there's no way that's true* — but そんなはずない is what comes out when someone's reacting on the spot, not writing something down. You'll hear it a lot; you just won't see it much in anything formal. Keep the full はずがない for writing and for polite conversation, and recognize はずない the instant someone blurts it out at you.

## Contrast

Line はず and はずがない up next to each other and the relationship is obvious — same core word, opposite conclusion, depending on nothing but which ending you pick.

```jp
彼[かれ]が来[く]るはずだ。
```

*He should be coming.*

```jp
彼[かれ]が来[く]るはずがない。
```

*There's no way he's coming.*

はずだ commits to *this should be true*, based on what you know. はずがない commits to *this cannot be true*, based on the exact same kind of knowledge pointed the other direction. Swap one for the other in the same sentence and you don't get a milder version of the same idea — you get the opposite claim, which is exactly why mixing them up in conversation gets noticed fast. There's no gentle middle setting on either of these — you don't reach for はず or はずがない when you're only leaning toward an answer. For that softer, more hedged territory, you'll want a different tool: らしい, built for exactly the situation where the evidence is a hint rather than a certainty, is coming up soon. For now, hold onto the gap between *should* and *can't* — it's the whole shape of this pattern.
caution_notes: はずがない needs a concrete reason behind it — used for a bare hunch with nothing backing it, it sounds far too forceful.
Attaching はずがない after an already-negative verb or adjective (ない form) flips the meaning to definitely must be true, not a stronger no way.
はずがありません is just the polite form of はずがない, not a separate pattern — pick based on politeness, not meaning.
In casual speech many people drop the が entirely (はずない); the meaning stays the same, only the register changes.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at your desk and notice your coworker's seat is empty, jacket gone from the hook. Someone mentions it over coffee, not with any real certainty — just passing along what they picked up secondhand. That's the exact gap らしい fills: a way to state something without claiming you personally confirmed it.

```jp
彼[かれ]は今日[きょう]休[やす]むらしい。
```

*I heard he's taking today off.*

You didn't check his calendar and you didn't call him. Someone told you, or you noticed something and pieced it together, and now you're reporting the conclusion rather than swearing to it. らしい carries that distance built right into the sentence — it's the difference between "he's off today" and "word is, he's off today."

This comes up constantly once you notice it. Weather, gossip, news you skimmed rather than read closely, a friend's plans you only heard about thirdhand — all of it wants らしい, because in all of it, you are not the source. English does the same job with "apparently," "supposedly," or "word is" — a small tag that quietly tells the listener where the information came from, without you having to spell it out in a whole extra sentence.

That's really the whole job of らしい: it lets one word carry a disclaimer that would otherwise take a full clause to say out loud ("I'm not totally sure, but from what I gather..."). Once you have it, you'll reach for it constantly, because most of what you know about other people's lives is secondhand anyway.

## How it works

らしい attaches after the **plain form** — the dictionary-style version of a word, the one you'd use with a close friend, not the polite -です/-ます version. With verbs, the plain dictionary form or the plain past slots straight in, no extra changes:

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]は先[せん]週[しゅう]旅[りょ]行[こう]に行[い]ったらしい。
```

*It seems my friend went on a trip last week.*

行[い]った already carries its own past tense on its back; らしい just tacks onto the end and adds "this is what I picked up, not what I watched happen."

い-adjectives work the same way — the plain adjective goes in exactly as it is:

```jp
あの店[みせ]の料[りょう]理[り]はおいしいらしい。
```

*That restaurant's food is apparently delicious.*

You haven't eaten there. Somebody who has told you, or you saw the line out the door and drew your own conclusion — either way, おいしい goes in untouched and らしい does the reporting.

な-adjectives and nouns are where people trip up, because these are exactly the words that normally lean on だ to finish a plain sentence. In front of らしい, that だ **disappears**:

```jp
新[あたら]しいレストランは有[ゆう]名[めい]らしい。
```

*The new restaurant is apparently famous.*

```jp
彼[かれ]は医[い]者[しゃ]らしい。
```

*He's apparently a doctor.*

有[ゆう]名[めい]だ becomes 有[ゆう]名[めい]らしい, not `有名だらしい`. 医[い]者[しゃ]だ becomes 医[い]者[しゃ]らしい, not `医者だらしい`. If your instinct is to slot だ in front of every だ-type word out of habit, this is the one place that habit has to switch off — らしい already behaves like an い-adjective itself, and い-adjectives never sit next to だ.

Negation works exactly the same way: whatever the plain negative form looks like — 忙[いそが]しくない, 休[やす]まない — らしい just attaches after it with no extra steps. Nothing about らしい itself changes; only the word underneath it does.

Put those pieces together and the rule is genuinely one rule, not four separate ones to memorize: find the plain form of whatever you're saying — verb, い-adjective, な-adjective, or noun — and drop らしい on the end. The only word class that needs a small adjustment is だ-type words, because だ itself has no place sitting in front of らしい.

## Rules and exceptions

> だ never survives in front of らしい, full stop. 静[しず]かだ → 静[しず]からしい, 学[がく]生[せい]だ → 学[がく]生[せい]らしい. Say `静かだらしい` out loud and it will sound exactly as wrong to a native speaker as it looks on the page.

らしい can stack です on the end for extra politeness, and this is completely normal: 忙[いそが]しいらしいです softens the claim while keeping the sentence polite. But the order only runs one way — らしい comes first, です after. `忙しいですらしい` is not something anyone says, in any register.

In casual speech among friends, らしい often gets a よ or a ね tacked onto the very end — 彼[かれ]は今日[きょう]休[やす]むらしいよ, 彼[かれ]は今日[きょう]休[やす]むらしいね — the way you'd add "you know" or "right?" in English. Neither particle changes what らしい itself is doing; they just color how the news lands, more of a nudge than a fact dump.

> There's a second, older job for this exact same word, and it's worth knowing before it confuses you. Noun + らしい can mean "typical of," not "seems to be." 子[こ]供[ども]らしい doesn't report a rumor about someone being a child — it means "childlike," acting the way a child would be expected to. 医[い]者[しゃ]らしい, said with nothing else around it, could mean "seems to be a doctor" or "acts like a proper doctor should." Whatever came right before it in the conversation is usually what tells you which one you're hearing.

Because らしい signals distance from the source, using it about something you witnessed with your own eyes tends to sound off — like you're hedging on a fact you're actually sure of. Save it for what you genuinely picked up secondhand, read somewhere, or pieced together from a clue, not for what you personally confirmed yourself.

That distinction matters more in Japanese than it might feel like it should in English, where "apparently" gets used loosely all the time, even about things we saw ourselves. A Japanese listener hearing らしい will assume, correctly, that you're not the source — so if you did see it happen, drop らしい entirely and just state the plain sentence. The absence of らしい is itself information.

## Contrast — らしい vs はず

You already have はず for "should be" — a conclusion you reasoned out yourself from something you already know. らしい covers the opposite direction: a conclusion that came from outside you, something you heard or noticed rather than worked out on your own.

```jp
空[そら]が暗[くら]いから、雨[あめ]が降[ふ]るはずだ。
```

*The sky is dark, so it should rain.*

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]が言[い]ったから、今日[きょう]の午[ご]後[ご]は雨[あめ]が降[ふ]るらしい。
```

*My friend told me, so it seems it'll rain this afternoon.*

Same weather, same conclusion, two completely different reasons for believing it. はず says "I looked at the evidence in front of me and worked this out myself." らしい says "someone else handed me this conclusion, and I'm passing it along." Mix the two up and you end up either claiming ownership of a guess that was never yours, or disowning one you actually reasoned through — both read strangely to a native listener, even if the sentence is grammatical.

らしい and はず don't stack together on the same claim; pick whichever one matches where the information actually came from, and let that choice do the talking.

A useful test when you're not sure which one to reach for: ask yourself whether you could explain *why* you believe the thing, using only your own knowledge, with no outside source involved. If yes, that's はず territory. If the honest answer is "someone told me" or "I noticed something and guessed," that's らしい, every time. The two patterns aren't really competing for the same sentences — they're sorting your beliefs by where they came from, and once you start asking that question automatically, the choice mostly makes itself.

Hold onto that distinction — a close cousin, ようだ, shows up soon, and it leans on your own read of a scene in front of you rather than something you were told about it.
caution_notes: だ always drops before らしい after nouns and な-adjectives — say 有名らしい and 医者らしい, never 有名だらしい or 医者だらしい.
If you add です for politeness, it goes after らしい, never before — 忙しいらしいです is fine, 忙しいですらしい is not.
Noun + らしい can mean "typical of" (子供らしい, childlike) instead of reporting something you heard, so surrounding context decides which meaning applies.
らしい signals you're not the source of the information, so using it about something you witnessed yourself can sound like you're hedging on a fact you're actually sure of.

items.explanation_markdown:
Picture this: you knock on a friend's door after texting them you'd stop by. No footsteps. No light spilling out from under the door. You wait a beat and knock again — still nothing. You don't actually know for a fact that they're out; nobody told you so, and you haven't called to check. You just have every reason to think so, based on what you can see and hear standing right there on the step.

That's exactly the job ようだ does. It's the grammar you reach for the moment you're drawing a conclusion from evidence sitting right in front of you — not stating a plain fact, not guessing out of nowhere, but reading a situation and saying, out loud, what it looks like from where you're standing.

```jp
誰[だれ]も家[いえ]にいないようだ。
```
*Looks like nobody's home.*

Notice the shape: the plain, everyday form of the verb — いない, meaning it doesn't exist here — with ようだ tacked on the end. That's the whole trick, and it holds for almost everything that follows. ようだ rides on top of the same plain form you already use talking casually with a friend, and it turns a flat statement into a read on the situation: here's what the evidence in front of me suggests.

## How it works

ようだ attaches after the plain form for verbs and i-adjectives, exactly as they already are — nothing new to memorize beyond what you already know. Na-adjectives and nouns each need one small adjustment, and those two are worth slowing down for:

- Verb, plain form (dictionary, past, or negative)
- I-adjective, plain form, unchanged
- Na-adjective, stem + な
- Noun + の

Start with a verb in its dictionary form, the same shape you'd use talking to a close friend. You look up and heavy grey clouds are building fast over the park:

```jp
雨[あめ]が降[ふ]るようだ。
```
*Looks like it's going to rain.*

Past tense works exactly the same way — just swap in the plain past form instead of the dictionary form. Nothing else in the sentence changes. You step outside later and the ground is dark and slick:

```jp
雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ったようだ。
```
*Looks like it rained.*

I-adjectives plug straight in with no changes at all — no だ to drop, nothing to swap. Everyone around the office has their coat zipped up to the chin and their hands jammed in their pockets:

```jp
今日[きょう]は寒[さむ]いようだ。
```
*Seems cold today.*

Na-adjectives are the one spot where the plain form needs a small correction, and it catches almost everyone the first time. A na-adjective's plain form technically ends in だ, as in 元[げん]気[き]だ or 暇[ひま]だ — but ようだ doesn't want that だ at all. It wants な instead, the exact same connector a na-adjective uses right before a noun, like 暇[ひま]な時[じ]間[かん] (free time).

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]は暇[ひま]なようだ。
```
*The teacher seems free.*

> Don't write `先生は暇だようだ` — that's the single most common slip with this pattern. Drop the だ, add な instead. It trips people up because every other plain form you've learned walks straight into ようだ completely unchanged; na-adjectives are the one exception.

Nouns get the same treatment as na-adjectives, but with の instead of な — this is the noun plus の plus ようだ shape written out formally, the one you'll see most often as the textbook version of this rule. Your friend opens the door pale, quiet, and barely upright, and you don't need them to say a word:

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]は病[びょう]気[き]のようだ。
```
*My friend seems to be sick.*

Swap だ for です anywhere in this whole pattern and you get the polite register, ようです — same evidence, same conclusion, nothing about the meaning changes, it's just dressed up for someone you don't know well, like a coworker or a stranger you're making conversation with:

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]は忙[いそが]しいようです。
```
*The teacher seems busy.*

## Rules and exceptions

The one non-negotiable ingredient here is evidence you picked up yourself — something you saw, heard, smelled, or otherwise noticed just now or very recently. ようだ is a conclusion drawn on the spot from something real in front of you, not a hunch pulled out of thin air and not a guess about something you have no way of checking.

That requirement also means ようだ sits oddly on facts you already know for certain about yourself. A sentence like 私[わたし]は学[がく]生[せい]のようだ is strange to a native ear — you don't need to read evidence that you're a student, you already know it without looking for clues. ようだ does show up talking about yourself, but mainly when you're noticing something about yourself as if from the outside — catching your reflection in a window and realizing you look worn out, say — not for plain, settled facts you'd never need to infer. The same logic applies to anything you already know firsthand: if you watched your friend walk in the door completely fine, you wouldn't turn around and say 友[とも]達[だち]は元[げん]気[き]なようだ about something you just witnessed directly with no room for doubt. Save ようだ for the gap between noticing something and being fully sure of it.

> ようだ describes what the evidence in front of you suggests, not what's already confirmed. The moment something becomes certain, the sentence usually drops ようだ entirely and just states it plainly.

## Casual speech

In relaxed, everyday speech, ようだ very often shrinks down to みたいだ, and you'll hear this constantly once you start listening for it. The meaning stays completely identical — same evidence, same conclusion, same level of confidence — but the attachment gets simpler across the board: no の, no な, みたいだ goes straight onto the noun or na-adjective with nothing in between.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]は病[びょう]気[き]みたいだ。
```
*My friend seems to be sick.*

> With みたいだ, skip の and な entirely — don't carry them over out of habit. `病気のみたいだ` and `暇なみたいだ` are both wrong; it's 病[びょう]気[き]みたいだ and 暇[ひま]みたいだ, full stop.

## Contrast: ようだ vs らしい

You've already met らしい, which also translates as seems, and the overlap is real enough that it trips people up for months. Here's the line between them: ようだ is your own impression, built from something you directly noticed — sight, sound, a scene playing out right in front of you. らしい leans on evidence that came from somewhere else entirely — something you heard secondhand, read, or were told by someone who saw it before you did.

Picture an empty platform with no train in sight for ten straight minutes, and you're the one standing there watching it not arrive:

```jp
電[でん]車[しゃ]が遅[おく]れたようだ。
```
*Looks like the train is delayed.*

Now picture hearing the exact same fact from a station announcement, or a text from a friend already waiting somewhere else, instead of watching it unfold with your own eyes:

```jp
電[でん]車[しゃ]が遅[おく]れたらしい。
```
*I heard the train is delayed.*

はず sits on a completely different axis from either of these. It's about what logically should be true given something you already trust as fact, not a fresh impression at all — closer to given what I already know, this has to be the case than here's what I'm noticing right now. ようだ never reaches that level of certainty; it's always sitting a half-step short of being sure, which is exactly why it's useful — it lets you say something without overcommitting to it. Mixing these three up mostly just sounds a little off rather than truly wrong, so don't panic if you blur them at first; the difference gets easier to feel the more often you notice, yourself, which kind of knowledge a sentence is actually resting on.

## Closing thought

Reading a situation and saying so, without overclaiming it, is most of what makes ようだ worth having in the first place — you'll reach for it constantly, the moment something looks, sounds, or feels a certain way and you want to say that out loud honestly instead of stating it as settled fact. みたいだ gets its own full lesson soon, with its own range of tone and use; for now, just recognize it as this exact same instinct, said a little more casually among friends.
caution_notes: Na-adjectives take な before ようだ, not だ — 暇なようだ is correct, not 暇だようだ.
With みたいだ, drop の and な entirely: it's 病気みたいだ and 暇みたいだ, never 病気のみたいだ or 暇なみたいだ.
ようだ needs evidence you personally noticed just now, so it sits oddly on facts you already know for certain about yourself.
ようだ marks your own impression from direct evidence, while らしい leans on secondhand information you heard or read.

You're at a friend's place for dinner, and they hand you a bowl of something they made themselves. It looks like an ordinary side dish — a little glossy, a little brown — nothing unusual on the surface. Then it hits your tongue and it's unmistakably sweet, like dessert wearing a dinner costume. You want to say something on the spot, casually, without stopping to construct a careful sentence first.

```jp
この料[りょう]理[り]はお菓[か]子[し]みたいだ。
```

*This dish tastes like candy.*

You could just say this is sweet — that's true, and it's simple — but that flattens the moment. What you actually want to report is the mismatch: it presents itself as one thing and turns out, as far as you can tell, to be another. English reaches for "seems like" or "tastes like" for exactly this job, and Japanese has a single, compact word that does the same work without any extra machinery.

That reaction — this looks, tastes, or feels like something else, going purely on your own impression in the moment — is exactly what みたいだ is built for. Attach it to the **plain form** (the casual, dictionary-style form you'd use with friends, not the polite -ます form) of almost anything, and an impression turns into a full sentence with barely any effort.

## How it works

みたいだ is easygoing about what it attaches to — nouns, na-adjectives, i-adjectives, and verbs all work, and for most of them the plain form is all you need, with nothing inserted in between.

With a noun, みたいだ just sits directly on top of it. お菓[か]子[し] (a sweet) plus みたいだ gives you exactly the sentence above — no connecting word, no extra syllable, nothing to remember except to keep them next to each other.

Na-adjectives lose something on the way in. Watch what happens to 静[しず]か (quiet):

```jp
静[しず]か → 静[しず]かみたいだ
```

*quiet → seems quiet*

```jp
この部屋[へや]は静[しず]かみたいだ。
```

*This room seems quiet.*

Notice what's missing: no な. A na-adjective normally needs that な right before a noun (静[しず]かな部屋[へや], a quiet room), but in front of みたいだ it drops out completely — みたいだ treats the na-adjective's bare stem the same way it treats a noun, so nothing extra gets inserted.

I-adjectives don't change at all. The form you'd find in a dictionary is the exact form you use:

```jp
あの料[りょう]理[り]は辛[から]いみたいだ。
```

*That dish looks spicy.*

Verbs behave the same way — plain form, completely untouched:

```jp
兄[あに]は晩[ばん]に出[で]るみたいだ。
```

*My older brother seems to be going out in the evening.*

Line them up and the shape is consistent:

- noun — bare, no connector (お菓[か]子[し]みたいだ)
- na-adjective — bare stem, no な (静[しず]かみたいだ)
- i-adjective — dictionary form, unchanged (辛[から]いみたいだ)
- verb — plain form, unchanged (出[で]るみたいだ)

One shape, four word types, nothing extra to memorize once you've seen it applied. For all four, swap だ for です whenever the company calls for it — あの料[りょう]理[り]は辛[から]いみたいです instead, same meaning, just dressed up a little for someone you don't know well.

## Rules and exceptions

The な that na-adjectives usually carry is the single most common slip here. `静かなみたいだ` feels like it should be right, because that な shows up everywhere else 静[しず]か goes — but not in front of みたいだ. Only 静[しず]かみたいだ is correct; the な simply has no job to do there.

> The same instinct causes trouble with nouns, usually from learners who've already met ようだ, which does take の after a noun. That の doesn't carry over: `料理のみたいだ` is wrong. みたいだ never takes の, on nouns or anything else.

It's tempting to reach for はず here instead, since you already have it for "should be" — but はず is about logical expectation, not appearance. はず fits when you've worked something out and expect it to be true; みたいだ fits when you're going purely on what's in front of you right now, no working-out required. The two can even show up describing the same situation and still disagree, because they're reporting two different kinds of confidence.

Plain みたいだ is casual by nature — perfectly fine with friends and family, a little blunt for a stranger, a client, or your boss. Reach for みたいです the moment the conversation turns more formal, the same way you'd reach for です anywhere else in the sentence.

The textbook line between "my own impression right now" (みたいだ), "something I heard or read" (らしい), and "what the evidence suggests" (ようだ) is cleaner on paper than it is in an actual conversation. Plenty of native speakers reach for みたいだ in all three situations and let context sort out which one they mean; noticing the categories blur in real speech is a sign you're paying attention, not a sign you're doing something wrong.

One more edge worth knowing: once you've actually confirmed what's going on — you've tasted the dish, you already know for a fact it's sweet — the guess disappears, and so does みたいだ. You'd just state the fact plainly, the same way you would in English once you'd stopped guessing and started knowing.

## Casual speech

In relaxed spoken Japanese, だ often disappears right before ね, especially once a sentence is basically just confirming something out loud to whoever's standing next to you.

```jp
雨[あめ]みたいだね。
```

*Looks like rain, doesn't it.*

```jp
雨[あめ]みたいね。
```

*Looks like rain, doesn't it.*

Both get used constantly; dropping the だ just sounds a touch more offhand, a little quicker off the tongue. Keep the だ in writing, or anywhere you want the sentence to stand on its own as a complete thought.

## Contrast

ようだ covers almost identical ground — an impression based on what you can see, hear, or otherwise sense — but it asks for more scaffolding on nouns and na-adjectives, and it reads more neutral, closer to something you'd write in a report than blurt out over dinner.

```jp
この料[りょう]理[り]はお菓[か]子[し]のようだ。
```

*This dish is like candy.*

Same dish, same idea as the sentence you opened with, but notice the の holding お菓[か]子[し] and ようだ together. That の is required with ようだ and forbidden with みたいだ — the single biggest thing to keep straight between the two once you know both. You'll meet ようだ constantly in writing and in anything read aloud for an audience — a script, an announcement over a station platform speaker — anywhere a sentence needs to sound composed rather than tossed off between friends. みたいだ almost never shows up in that kind of formal delivery; it belongs to conversation, texts, anywhere you'd talk the way you actually talk.

らしい lives in a different lane entirely: it's for something you picked up secondhand — a forecast on the news, a rumor, something someone told you — not something you're sensing with your own eyes or ears right now.

```jp
明日[あした]は雨[あめ]らしい。
```

*I heard it's going to rain tomorrow.*

Say that after checking the forecast. Look up at a darkening sky yourself and reach for みたいだ instead — same rain, but the confidence behind the sentence comes from a completely different place. らしい answers "where did you get this," while みたいだ answers "what does it look like to you, right now."

Once the shape settles in, みたいだ turns into one of the most-used sentence-enders you own, because most of what you notice about the world around you really is exactly that: a first impression, not a certified fact. Most of language learning early on is just this — noticing how often you're actually reporting an impression instead of a fact, and finally having a word ready for it. Hold onto that instinct: once ている (marking something as ongoing) enters the picture, you'll be able to say what someone looks like they're doing, not just what they look like.
caution_notes: Don't add な before みたいだ after a na-adjective, like in 静かなみたいだ — go straight to 静かみたいだ.
Don't add の before みたいだ after a noun the way you would with ようだ, like in 料理のみたいだ — say 料理みたいだ instead.
みたいだ on its own is casual; switch to みたいです once the conversation turns formal.
らしい points to something you heard or read, while みたいだ points to your own impression right now — keep them apart.
